papers.abstract: Applications such as visual accessibility agents and robotics require answering questions about recent video content promptly, over a bounded window of past frames (e.g., the last two minutes). Hybrid vision-language models (VLMs), which interleave attention with linear recurrent layers such as Gated DeltaNet (GDN), are attractive for this setting, but maintaining a sliding window is expensive. The reason is that recurrent layers combine all past frames into a shared state, so expiring old frames normally requires re-running the entire window through the model. We observe that the recurrent update is affine in the state with input-dependent coefficients, so the effect of each frame can be captured as a transformation that composes associatively. We present Spool, a training-free framework that caches per-frame state transformations and composes them efficiently as the window advances, removing expired frames from each recurrent layer's state without replaying frames through the backbone. Removal is exact within each layer; as with key-value eviction in attention, expired frames can retain residual influence through the cached inputs computed by earlier layers. We design a dedicated data structure and GPU kernels to achieve low caching and composition overhead. Across five open-source hybrid VLMs and four video reasoning benchmarks, Spool achieves the lowest p95 time-to-first-token in all 20 model-benchmark tests, reducing it by a geometric mean of $6.6\times$ over the faster of two recent vLLM baselines, while improving accuracy by 2.3 percentage points on average.
authors: Rui Ning, Om Chabra, Hari Balakrishnan
bullets: Targets prompt responses for video-based agents operating over bounded histories.
Caches each frame’s recurrent-state transformation and composes transformations associatively as the window advances.
Uses a specialized data structure and GPU kernels to limit caching and composition overhead.
Across five hybrid VLMs and four benchmarks, it achieved the lowest p95 time-to-first-token in all 20 tests.
Reduced p95 time-to-first-token by 6.6× on average versus the faster of two vLLM baselines, while improving accuracy by 2.3 percentage points on average.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Architecture of the hybrid VLM. Multiple input frames are converted into visual tokens by a vision encoder and passed alongside text tokens into a unified backbone. This backbone interleaves recurrent layers, which update a fixed-size state for each token, with attention layers, which retain per-token key–value entries.

Figure 8. Mean GDN state error. Relative Frobenius error averaged over each model’s GDN layers, comparing Spool with Spool without reconstruction against the vLLM reference. The evaluation uses all 9,000 Beyond3D questions.

Figure 1. Spool maintains a sliding video window without replaying retained frames. (a) Shifting the window retains four of five frames. (b) Prefix-cache invalidation forces the retained context to be rebuilt. (c) Spool composes cached recurrent transformations and reclaims key–value slots by moving surviving tail entries into holes left by eviction.

Figure 4. Efficient recurrent-state reconstruction with cached transformations. Spool caches each block’s affine state transformation and then replays them without the effect of a given block. A segment tree composes consecutive transformations, enabling reconstruction of the active window in O(logW ) operations. In this example, frames 5–8 occupy cyclic slots 1–3 and 0, with frame 8 wrapping around to slot 0. Spool first applies F5, then the combined transformation F6,7, and finally F8 to the prefix state Sp. This recovers the window state using only three cached transformations, without reprocessing video tokens or updating the tree during reconstruction.

Parentheses: speedup over the faster baseline.

papers.abstract: Human visual reasoning is driven by systematic exploration and extraction of task-relevant visual evidence. Human gaze provides a window into this process, making gaze a useful source of guidance for visually-grounded reasoning in vision-language models (VLMs). However, human gaze also includes noise and redundancies that may transfer poorly to VLMs. In this work, we investigate how human gaze data can be effectively leveraged to improve visual reasoning in VLMs, while maintaining alignment with human behavior. We collect 7,109 human gaze trials from a diverse and challenging set of visual reasoning tasks, and train grounded reasoning models with different forms of gaze guidance. Across evaluations in chart understanding, visual search, and counting, we find that using human gaze as a prior for grounded reasoning consistently outperforms supervision using the full gaze sequence. Based on these findings, we introduce GGR (Gaze-Guided Reasoner), which achieves greater human alignment and more reliable visual grounding while matching or outperforming leading grounded-reasoning baselines in accuracy. Reinforcement learning further improves task accuracy, gaze alignment, and grounding quality despite using no gaze supervision. Behavioral analyses show that gaze supervised models exhibit more visual exploration before arriving at an answer. Our results suggest that the value of human gaze lies in guiding spatial exploration and shaping reasoning behavior without requiring complete imitation of human behavior.
authors: Gabriel Sarch, Declan Campbell, Nicholas Budny, Kia Ghods, Katerina Fragkiadaki, Jonathan D. Cohen, Brenden M. Lake, Taylor W. Webb
bullets: Collects 7,109 human gaze trials across challenging visual reasoning tasks.
Tests gaze guidance for chart understanding, visual search, and counting.

Reinforcement learning further improves accuracy, gaze alignment, and grounding without gaze supervision.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) can provide harmful assistance by interpreting visual events, even without an explicit request for the underlying harmful objective. We identify this \textbf{scene-state safety vulnerability} and introduce \textbf{SceneSafetyBench}, comprising 375 image--question pairs spanning Initial, Medium, and Ultimate scene states and five visual presentations. Across eight VLMs, scene-state inputs elicit harmful assistance with attack success rates (ASRs) of 45.6--72.3\%. Comparative analysis across three VLMs shows that scene-state inputs most closely resemble QR-related images in their layer-wise safety-related signal profiles, while exhibiting lower average late-layer readouts and distinct signal dynamics during generation. To turn this vulnerability into a systematic attack, we propose \textbf{S3TA}, which translates harmful objectives into scene states, queries image--question pairs independently, and assembles the responses. On seven MM-SafetyBench categories across eight open-weight and commercial VLMs, S3TA achieves a model-average ASR of \textbf{71.2\%, exceeding the strongest baseline by 6.1 percentage points}. Text-side filters and visual moderation provide limited protection. These findings highlight the need to safeguard the assistance models infer through scene-grounded reasoning, beyond screening input content.
authors: Tongxi Wu, Yuyang Cheng, Jiacheng Xian, Menglin Yang, Kai Chen, Jian Zhang, Yang Gao
bullets: Introduces scene-state safety vulnerability: models may infer and assist with harmful objectives from visual events without explicit harmful requests.

S3TA achieved a 71.2% model-average attack success rate, 6.1 percentage points above the strongest baseline; text and visual filters offered limited protection.

papers.abstract: Preference optimization (PO) is the standard way to reduce object hallucination in large vision-language models. We find that four public PO checkpoints of LLaVA-1.5-7B also lower object coverage. They name fewer object categories, and their lower hallucination rates bring no significant gain in set-level object F1 on CHAIR. We therefore ask how much of the PO gain the base model can reproduce by stopping earlier. A positive end-of-sequence (EOS) logit bias lets the base model reach the recall of each PO model, and this early stopping alone reproduces 58 to 86 percent of the CHAIRi gain of three checkpoints on two disjoint COCO sets. Writing longer does not bring the lost categories back. Under greedy decoding, a negative EOS bias recovers only 2 to 9 percent of the lost CHAIR recall of these checkpoints, and 94 to 96 percent of the added object mentions repeat categories already named. On CHAIR, the base caption of the same image still names about half of the missed object categories. We therefore propose base-guided object-category restoration, which appends high-confidence base-only categories to the PO caption without training. With thresholds fixed on a development set, it brings three checkpoints within one point of the base recall on a held-out COCO set with a lower distinct-object hallucination rate than the base model. Against the recall-matched base stopping curve, its gain holds for RLAIF-V near the base recall and for RLAIF-V and CHAIR-DPO at an intermediate recall. We will release the code of the recall-controlled evaluation.
bullets: Four public preference-optimized checkpoints name fewer object categories and show no significant set-level object F1 improvement on CHAIR.
A positive EOS logit bias makes the base model stop earlier and reproduces 58–86% of three checkpoints’ CHAIRi gains across two COCO sets.
Longer decoding does not restore the categories lost by preference optimization; negative EOS bias recovers little of the lost recall, with most added mentions repeating existing categories.
The proposed base-guided object-category restoration appends high-confidence categories absent from the optimized caption.
With development-set thresholds, restoration approaches base-model recall on held-out COCO while maintaining a lower distinct-object hallucination rate.

papers.tldr: Preference optimization reduces object hallucinations in LLaVA-1.5-7B partly by saying fewer objects, but base-guided restoration can recover missed categories without training while keeping hallucination lower than the base model.

papers.abstract: Video question answering under tight frame budgets requires preserving localized motion and event order, yet current video multimodal large language models (MLLMs) reduce comprehension to static multi-image reasoning by discarding unselected frames and encoding keyframes independently: (1) Spatially, whole-frame pooling dilutes small moving targets into static backgrounds; (2) Temporally, dropping intermediate frames or averaging tokens erases inter-frame motion, confusing direction, speed, and order. We propose VIVID (Visual Inter-frame Variations and Individual Dynamics), which moves beyond static snapshots like human vision: keyframes capture core states while inter-frame Patch Diffs preserve neighboring changes within $K_f$ keyframes. Autonomous Delta-Driven Keyframe Planning (ADKP) selects anchors from a $3\text{ fps}$ pool and feeds surrounding patch differences into Dual-Road Change Memory (DRCM), forming Dynamic Tokens at zero extra anchor tokens alongside a camera-stabilized Active Motion Region of Interest (ROI) and chronological Entity State Chains. Adding $0.22\%$ trainable parameters to a frozen $27\text{B}$ backbone, VIVID-Small ($50$ examples, $\sim 1.5$ GPU hours) beats all eleven baselines in overall accuracy across $8,083$ questions and trails only VIVID-Large ($3,600$ examples), which leads on MotionBench, Video-MME, and TempCompass.
authors: Chengqian Ma, Yuanze Zeng, Hongyu Wang, Mingfeng Lin, YiCheng Xiao, Yu Chen, Pengyu Li, WenHao Wang, Yuexiao Ma, Xiawu Zheng, Fei Chao
bullets: Addresses spatial dilution of small moving objects and temporal loss of motion direction, speed, and event order.
Uses Delta-Driven Keyframe Planning to select anchors, while Patch Diffs encode changes between neighboring frames.
Dual-Road Change Memory, active motion ROIs, and Entity State Chains form dynamic, temporally ordered representations.
With only 0.22% trainable parameters on a frozen 27B backbone, VIVID-Small outperforms eleven baselines overall across 8,083 questions.
VIVID-Large achieves the strongest results on MotionBench, Video-MME, and TempCompass; the method is evaluated under limited-data settings.

papers.abstract: Retrieval-augmented vision-language models (VLMs) answer from two sources of evidence that can each fail: the retrieved text can be wrong or noisy, and the image can be degraded or contradicted. We introduce GIB-200K, 200,000 image-question items built from COCO and Visual Genome, each expanded into controlled stress conditions: hard-negative retrieval noise (1-20 documents), visual ambiguity (Gaussian and motion blur, low-resource crops) and cross-modal conflict with counterfactual flip pairs. Instead of only measuring degradation, we ask how models combine the two modalities. From ideal Bayesian cue combination we derive a testable prediction that yields formal definitions of Knowledge Inertia (text over-weighted relative to the model's own image evidence) and Sensory Capture (the reverse), and we estimate the weights with a measurement-error-corrected regression whose recovery of known weights we verify. A counterfactual flip decomposition separates modality bias from concept priors, and a Grounding Illusion Score measures how much clean accuracy is not grounded in the image. We evaluate 4 open models on one frozen, seeded evaluation split of 2,000 GIB-200K items. All models are accurate on clean inputs (92.5%-94.2%) but adverse accuracy falls to 41.3%-59.9%. The two LLaVA models over-weight the text (Knowledge Inertia, w_T/w_I = 1.229 and 1.322), whereas InternVL3 favours the image (w_T/w_I = 0.680); between 34.8% and 71.4% of the clean answers that are correct are abandoned when the document lies. A training-free consistency check that compares the answer with and without retrieval trades coverage for accuracy under misleading documents, while falling back to the image fails when the image is heavily degraded. All per-instance outputs, code, and an audit that recomputes every reported open-model number are released.
bullets: Introduces GIB-200K, a benchmark of controlled retrieval noise, image degradation, and cross-modal conflicts.
Derives measures for text over-weighting (Knowledge Inertia), image over-weighting (Sensory Capture), and ungrounded clean accuracy (Grounding Illusion Score).
Evaluates four open models using measurement-error-corrected regression and counterfactual flip analysis.
Clean accuracy is high (92.5%–94.2%) but drops substantially under adverse conditions (41.3%–59.9%).
A retrieval consistency check improves reliability under misleading documents at the cost of coverage; image fallback is unreliable when images are degraded.

papers.title: The Illusion of Grounding: Do Vision-Language Models Weigh Retrieved Text and Images Like an Ideal Observer?
papers.tldr: The study shows that vision-language models often combine retrieved text and images non-ideally, becoming over-reliant on one modality when the other is noisy or contradictory.

papers.abstract: Long-video question answering benchmarks like Video-MME-v2 typically evaluate systems under a uniform frame budget for every question, despite stark variation in the evidence each query actually demands. We analyze this mismatch on Video-MME-v2 and find that different question subsets prefer different frozen frame-budget policies, while uniformly increasing the frame count does not reliably improve all metrics. These findings motivate fixed-mean frame-budget routing, a controlled inference setting in which each question may receive a different frame budget while the average budget matches a uniform reference. We introduce FrameRouter, a training-free test-time framework that combines an evidence-demand router, a budget-constrained allocation rule, and a frozen bank of frame-sampling policies. By controlling how much visual evidence each question receives while leaving the underlying samplers unchanged, FrameRouter is orthogonal to query-aware frame selection. Across Video-MME-v2 and several long-video understanding benchmarks, FrameRouter improves long-video question answering by using the same average visual budget more selectively across questions. Code is available at https://github.com/bingjunluo/FrameRouter.
authors: Bingjun Luo, Jialin Guo, Siqi Li
bullets: Uniform frame budgets overlook variation in how much visual evidence different questions require.
The authors find that question subsets favor different frozen frame-sampling policies, and more frames do not consistently improve every metric.
FrameRouter is a training-free test-time framework with an evidence-demand router, budget-constrained allocation, and frozen sampling-policy bank.
It keeps the average visual budget equal to a uniform reference while reallocating frames selectively across questions.
Experiments on Video-MME-v2 and other long-video benchmarks show improved QA performance without changing the underlying samplers.

papers.title: FrameRouter: Frame Budget Routing for Long-Video Understanding on Video-MME-v2 and Beyond
papers.tldr: FrameRouter improves long-video QA by routing a fixed average frame budget to each question according to its evidence needs.

papers.abstract: Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation (MOPD) enables a single student to absorb the skills of several domain teachers by learning from its own generated responses. We present Multimodal Model Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation Reasoner (M3OPD-Reasoner), a fully open recipe for post-training vision-language models (VLMs) over three reasoning domains: image STEM, image perception, and video. We curate two datasets, M3OPD-SFT-1.35M for supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and M3OPD-RL-193K for reinforcement learning (RL) with verifiable rewards. On these data, we compare post-training recipes that start from Qwen3.5-9B: training one model on the mixed data of all domains (MixSFT and MixRL), and training one teacher per domain with Group Sequence Policy Optimization (GSPO), directly or after an SFT warm-up, and distilling the teachers into one student with MOPD. We evaluate on 21 image STEM, image perception, and video reasoning benchmarks after we decontaminate the training data against them. The comparison establishes MOPD of teachers trained with GSPO directly from Qwen3.5-9B as the best recipe: the student closely matches each teacher on its own domain and is on average above the mixed-training baselines on the same prompts. Since MOPD already merges the domain capabilities that MixRL would otherwise have to learn, its student is a stronger starting point for RL, and we ask whether the same data can carry the model further from there: we add MixRL on top of the MOPD student, on the same prompts and with the same settings, which, to our knowledge, no prior VLM recipe has studied. The same prompts still improve the MOPD student, with no collapse, and give our main model, M3OPD-Reasoner-9B. MOPD and MixRL can therefore work as consecutive stages that get more out of the same data. We release all data, the training code, and the checkpoints of every stage.
authors: Nguyen Quang Trung, Hoang Phan, Shuo Sun, Longyin Zhang, AiTi Aw
bullets: Targets multimodal reasoning across image STEM, image perception, and video domains.
Uses domain-specific GSPO-trained teachers and Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation (MOPD) to merge their capabilities into one student.
Introduces M3OPD-SFT-1.35M and M3OPD-RL-193K, with verifiable rewards, and evaluates on 21 decontaminated benchmarks.
MOPD outperforms mixed-training baselines on average while closely matching each teacher in its specialized domain.
A subsequent MixRL stage further improves the MOPD student without collapse, producing M3OPD-Reasoner-9B; data, code, and checkpoints are released.

papers.title: M3OPD-Reasoner: An Open Recipe for Post-Training Multimodal Reasoning with Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation

papers.abstract: Ensembles of diverse Large Vision Language Models have demonstrated performance beyond that of single models across multiple datasets and tasks. However, the necessary aggregation process usually relies on training, parameter fitting, or complex task-specific pipelines. Furthermore, evaluation is limited, making a fair comparison difficult. We create a unified pipeline where we perform candidate response selection: we build an ensemble by selecting the best answer from a set provided by different models. We comprehensively evaluate across 34 different means of confidence estimation, 24 ensemble configurations, 20 datasets, and two prompt specifications. We show that simple training and parameter-free approaches can be sufficient, even for ensembles of different architectures. These simple self-assessment approaches rely solely on each constituent model's confidence, without explicit calibration, yet are able to perform better than said constituent models. They are also competitive with more involved alternatives on standard metrics such as accuracy, including on open-ended problems. However, we also discover that dataset, ensemble composition, and prompt wording are key confounding variables insufficiently explored by prior work that significantly affect ensemble performance, such that the ensemble can perform worse than its best constituent model. These must be optimized for to get the most out of ensembles, at the cost of limiting their generalizability. We recommend that practitioners consider training-free ensembles only if deployment conditions can be precisely characterized, with Best-of-N configurations of strong models being a good starting point.
bullets: The study uses candidate response selection to choose the best answer from responses generated by multiple LVLMs.
It evaluates 34 confidence-estimation methods, 24 ensemble configurations, 20 datasets, and two prompt specifications.
Training-free, parameter-free self-assessment can outperform individual constituent models and remain competitive with more complex methods, including on open-ended tasks.
Ensembles may underperform their best constituent model when dataset, model composition, or prompt conditions are poorly matched.
The authors recommend training-free ensembles when deployment conditions are well characterized, with Best-of-N strong-model setups as a starting point.

papers.abstract: Omni-modal large language models (OLLMs) provide joint multimodal understanding and generation capabilities, making them well-suited to complex environments and promising backbones for next-generation AI. Despite these advances, the harmful stereotypes encoded in such models manifest in increasingly diverse forms, leading to broader and more severe societal consequences. Existing debiasing methods typically impose separate fairness objectives for each sensitive attribute and modality to minimise demographic-dependent variations. However, in omni-modal settings, this attribute-centric paradigm struggles to jointly address diverse social biases with distinct fairness objectives and to generalise beyond predefined attributes. To this end, we propose OmniDebias, one of the first methods for promoting fairness in OLLMs, which employs a bias-centric formulation to extract and mitigate a shared bias representation across attributes and modalities while preserving attribute-related knowledge. Specifically, we exploit activation inconsistencies of a given attribute (e.g., gender) across semantic contexts (e.g., occupations) to disentangle bias from legitimate knowledge. We further consolidate multiple extracted biases into a shared representation, formulating a unified objective that captures the underlying structure across social biases and generalises to unseen attributes. Extensive experiments demonstrate that eliminating unified bias with both post-hoc editing and fine-tuning can consistently improve fairness across diverse attributes and modalities in OLLMs while maintaining favourable utility.
authors: Runqi Lin, Suqin Yuan, Zihao Fu, Chris Russell
bullets: Existing attribute- and modality-specific debiasing struggles with diverse biases and unseen sensitive attributes.
OmniDebias extracts bias from activation inconsistencies across semantic contexts while retaining legitimate attribute-related knowledge.
It consolidates multiple biases into a unified representation and objective spanning attributes and modalities.
Post-hoc editing and fine-tuning consistently improve fairness across diverse attributes and modalities while maintaining favourable utility.

Bias-centric methods instead disentangle and mitigate shared bias while preserving legitimate attribute-related knowledge, enabling unified debiasing across attributes and modalities and facilitating generalisation to unseen attributes.

papers.abstract: Scientific document reasoning requires an agent to acquire and integrate evidence distributed across text, figures, and tables. Retrieval can identify relevant sources while missing complementary support, and answer-level feedback alone does not reveal whether an error stems from evidence acquisition or evidence use. We present an agentic Retriever--Perceiver--Reasoner framework for multimodal scientific document reasoning. The Retriever sequentially selects source-aligned evidence under a context budget. Given the selected evidence and question, the Perceiver constructs a question-conditioned latent ontology, an implicit organization of multimodal evidence in a shared continuous space. The Reasoner combines this latent guidance with the original sources to produce grounded answers. We train the three components through diagnostic-guided co-evolution: alternating updates optimize them with a shared answering reward, while Retrieval Potential Feedback (RPF) and Latent Efficacy Feedback (LEF) identify questions that need better retrieval or latent guidance and direct targeted resampling. Across four benchmarks and seven evaluation settings, our framework obtains average scores of 69.9 and 75.0 with 7B and 8B Reasoner backbones, exceeding the strongest baseline by 4.0 and 9.1 points, respectively.
authors: Frank Nie, Ethan B. Liu, Yuan Zhu, Jindong Han
bullets: Targets reasoning over evidence distributed across text, figures, and tables, where retrieval and evidence use can fail separately.
The Retriever selects source-aligned evidence under a context budget, while the Perceiver builds a question-conditioned latent ontology.
The Reasoner combines latent guidance with original sources to generate grounded answers.
Diagnostic-guided co-evolution uses shared answering rewards plus Retrieval Potential Feedback and Latent Efficacy Feedback for targeted updates.
Across four benchmarks and seven settings, it achieves average scores of 69.9 with a 7B backbone and 75.0 with an 8B backbone, outperforming the strongest baseline by 4.0 and 9.1 points.

figures.caption: Figure 1. Motivation and overview of our agentic framework. Diagnostic-guided co-evolution further coordinates evidence acquisition and utilization through a shared answering reward and paired diagnostics.

Figure 2. Overview of diagnostic-guided co-evolution. (1) Diagnostic-guided resampling combines regular questions with RPF- or LEFselected questions for component-specific training. (2) Alternating component co-adaptation sequentially updates the Perceiver, Retriever, and Reasoner under a shared answering reward, keeping the other two components fixed at each update. (3) Paired diagnostic feedback uses RPF to compare responses based on retrieved and annotated evidence, and LEF to compare responses with and without latent guidance. Positive score gaps determine the feedback pools for the next training cycle.

papers.abstract: We show that an appropriate visual harness can substantially improve the performance of general vision-language models (VLMs) across diverse medical imaging tasks. We introduce \ours, a medical visual harness that equips general VLMs with interactive visual tools and systematic diagnostic evidence management. With \ours, general VLMs interactively explore medical images and progressively acquire diagnostic evidence, which is preserved in a lossless memory for subsequent retrieval and use. After submitting an initial answer, the VLM receives an assessment of potential omissions and the reliability of identified findings. This assessment guides further image inspection and measurement, followed by answer revision in an iterative agentic loop until sufficient evidence is obtained. Across 11 tasks and four imaging modalities, \ours improves performance on all tasks with Qwen3.8-27B, with notable gains in spleen measurement (63.3\% to 98.3\%), renal search (57.5\% to 71.2\%), and pulmonary nodule detection (0.0\% to 28.2\%). High-capability API-based VLMs achieve even higher performance with \ours. For example, GPT-6.1 Sol improves pulmonary nodule detection from 10.8\% to 69.2\% with \ours, demonstrating the complementary benefits of stronger model capabilities and an effective medical visual harness. Our results highlight the potential of visual harnesses as a new paradigm for scaling general VLMs to medical imaging tasks.
authors: Shaowen Wan, Hanqi Jiang, Zihao Wu, Junhao Chen, Weihang You, Ruiyu Yan, Bowen Chen, Tianming Liu, Lin Zhao
bullets: Addresses the challenge of adapting general VLMs to diverse medical image analysis tasks.

Higher-capability API-based VLMs also benefit, suggesting complementary effects between model strength and the visual harness.

papers.abstract: Looped vision-language models (VLMs) deepen computation by reusing shared layers, approaching larger models' capabilities with fewer parameters and easing the storage and deployment burden of stacking independent layers. However, repeatedly processing long visual sequences still incurs substantial compute and GPU memory costs. Visual token compression reduces these costs by shortening sequences. Existing methods mainly select original tokens directly or combine selection with aggregation. In looped models, the former may overlook changing token importance across calls and discard information needed later; the latter lack joint consideration of output changes across calls, limiting information preservation. We propose LoopZip, a training-free visual token compression algorithm addressing both issues. Visual aggregation builds a compact candidate pool before the looped backbone, and cross-invocation selection averages instruction attention from the first two existing calls of the same shared attention layer to retain tokens needed by both states. Weight-tied value correction then jointly fits shared visual-value adjustments to both pre-selection layer outputs, reducing output deviations across states. To validate LoopZip's effectiveness, we conduct extensive experiments covering two open-source looped VLMs, eleven benchmarks, and three pruning ratios. On LoopVL-1B, LoopZip retains 97.16% of the original model's performance at 50% pruning ratio and exceeds the strongest baseline by 5.36% at 87.5% pruning ratio. Across Hugging Face Transformers, vLLM, and SGLang, LoopVL-1B with LoopZip reduces peak allocated GPU memory by 58.36%-58.98% and achieves 2.01-2.47x end-to-end speedups over the original model.
authors: Weizhong Huang, Zhicheng Liu, Yan Zhang, Fei Chao, Xiawu Zheng, Liujuan Cao
bullets: Targets the high compute and GPU-memory cost of repeatedly processing long visual-token sequences in looped VLMs.
Builds a compact candidate pool through visual aggregation before the looped backbone.
Selects tokens using averaged instruction attention from the first two calls of shared layers, capturing changing token importance across states.
Applies weight-tied value correction to reduce output deviations after pruning.

Across two looped VLMs and eleven benchmarks, it retains 97.16% performance at 50% pruning and delivers up to 58.98% lower peak GPU memory and 2.47× speedup; scope is limited to the evaluated models, benchmarks, and pruning ratios.
papers.selection_reason: Visual token compression for looped vision-language models; combines token pruning with cross-invocation selection and reduces memory/compute in VLMs.
papers.title: LoopZip: Visual Token Compression for Efficient Looped Vision-Language Models
papers.tldr: LoopZip is a training-free visual-token compression method for looped VLMs that preserves performance while substantially reducing memory use and inference time.

papers.abstract: Online vision-language models often miss small details in large images, because the service shrinks the image, or rejects it, before the model ever sees it. A car 20 pixels wide in an 8000 by 6000 drone photo reaches Claude about 6 pixels wide, and OpenAI's default rejects the photo outright. We measure how much detail survives for seven models from four vendors, using an eye exam of printed codes and 601 questions about small objects in real photos. The smallest text a model reads half the time grows from 6 pixels or less on a small image to a predicted 10 to 13 pixels on a 7680 by 4320 photo at default settings. Zooming wins much of the detail back. Splitting each photo into up to nine tiles raises accuracy by 11.1 to 14.5 percentage points for Claude and Gemini, and by avoiding rejections it lifts GPT-6.1 Sol from 50.7% to 83.7%. A two-step zoom, in which the model first names the region it needs, matches or beats tiles on Gemini and comes within 2.5 points of them on Claude, with about 40% of their image tokens. When a detail is lost, Claude and Gemini both say they cannot tell about half the time, but they fail differently in the rest: Gemini gives a confident wrong answer in 43% to 48% of these cases, Claude in only 5% to 9%. A check based on detail size, run before the call, misses most of the gain from tiles on Claude and Gemini, but Claude's own reply is a reliable trigger: tiling only after an unsure reply comes within 1.4 points of always tiling with 62% to 70% of the image tokens. We turn these findings into five rules for when an agent should zoom, and release the eye exam, every model answer and code at https://siddvoh.com/know-when-to-zoom.
bullets: Evaluates seven models from four vendors using printed-code tests and 601 real-photo questions about small objects.
At default settings, readable text thresholds rise from ≤6 pixels on small images to an estimated 10–13 pixels on 7680×4320 images.
Splitting images into up to nine tiles improves Claude and Gemini accuracy by 11.1–14.5 percentage points and raises GPT-6.1 Sol from 50.7% to 83.7% by avoiding rejections.
A two-step zoom—asking the model to identify the needed region before cropping—matches or nearly matches tiling on Claude and Gemini with about 40% of the image tokens.
Models differ in uncertainty: Gemini is confidently wrong more often than Claude when details are unavailable; Claude’s unsure replies can effectively trigger selective tiling.

papers.selection_reason: Empirical study of vision-language model limitations on small details and zooming/tiling strategies; relevant to multimodal LLM behavior.
papers.title: Know When to Zoom: How Small Is Too Small for Vision-Language Models?
papers.tldr: Large images hide small details from vision-language models, but adaptive zooming can recover much of the lost accuracy while using fewer image tokens than always tiling.

papers.abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have excelled in Western medical imaging, yet their potential in Traditional Chinese Medicine (TCM) tongue diagnosis remains systematically unevaluated. Tongue diagnosis requires sophisticated global and local perception, serving as a rigorous touchstone for assessing the visual understanding depth of MLLMs. However, existing datasets are limited by single dimensions, coarse granularity, and ambiguous labels, hindering the evaluation of authentic clinical capabilities. To bridge this gap, we introduce OmniTongue, the first comprehensive, fine-grained Visual Question Answering benchmark for TCM tongue diagnosis. This benchmark integrates 1,351 expert-validated images and 21,616 instruction pairs. Its core design features 16 clinical dimensions for multidimensional evaluation, region-specific annotations for pathological localization, and 66 fine-grained labels for precise diagnostic representation. Extensive evaluations of existing MLLMs reveal significant performance gaps, demonstrating that medical-specific models lack domain advantages, while universally poor Macro-F1 scores expose a reliance on statistical shortcuts rather than genuine understanding of tongue pathology. These findings not only highlight the current limitations of MLLMs in interpreting regional medical features but also underscore OmniTongue's significance for developing robust automated tongue diagnosis models. The code and dataset will be made publicly available in a future release.
authors: Liuyi Xu, Yun Guo, Shusheng Li, Xuewen Zhang, Yining Qian, An-Yang Lu
bullets: Addresses the lack of systematic evaluation for MLLMs in Traditional Chinese Medicine tongue diagnosis.
Provides 1,351 expert-validated images and 21,616 instruction pairs in a Visual Question Answering benchmark.
Evaluates 16 clinical dimensions with region-specific annotations and 66 fine-grained diagnostic labels.
Tests existing MLLMs and finds significant performance gaps, including universally poor Macro-F1 scores that suggest reliance on statistical shortcuts.
Code and dataset are planned for public release; current findings focus on evaluation rather than a new diagnostic model.

Table 3. Regional Perception Assessment: Benchmark results on OmniTongue for Comprehensive Regional Coating Features (Macro-F1 / Acc %). This evaluates models’ spatial grounding and diagnostic precision across the Root (R: Kidney), Middle (M: Spleen/Stomach), and Tip (T: Heart/Lung) anatomical zones.

Table 1. Global Perception Assessment (I): Benchmark results on OmniTongue for Global Tongue Body Features (Macro-F1 / Acc %). This evaluates the model’s ability to capture holistic morphological and chromatic attributes.

papers.selection_reason: Multimodal LLM benchmark for fine-grained visual understanding and instruction following.
papers.title: OmniTongue: A Comprehensive MLLM Benchmark for Automated Tongue Diagnosis in Traditional Chinese Medicine
papers.tldr: OmniTongue introduces a fine-grained benchmark showing that current MLLMs struggle with genuine, region-aware TCM tongue diagnosis.

papers.abstract: Omni Models process audio, vision, and text within a unified language backbone, yet often produce different answers for semantically equivalent inputs across modalities. Existing representation-level analyses do not distinguish between information that predicts whether disagreement will occur and the representation whose perturbation affects the model's answer. In this paper, we estimate a low-dimensional Answer Subspace from answer-position representations and use it to separate answer-related components from the remaining representation. Across three Omni Models and two multimodal reasoning tasks, information predictive of cross-modal inconsistency lies mainly outside the Answer Subspace, concentrating in a reproducible two-dimensional representation that is not explained by a fixed modality offset. Matched interventions reveal distinct behavioral roles: perturbing the Answer Subspace substantially changes the model's predictions, whereas perturbing the disagreement representation, like a random subspace of the same dimensionality, leaves them almost unchanged. Our key finding is that cross-modal disagreement can be induced by misaligning modality-specific answer representations: perturbing the Answer Subspace for only one modality induces disagreement, whereas applying the same perturbation to both largely preserves agreement. Thus, the representation that predicts disagreement is distinct from the answer-level representation through which disagreement can be induced, showing that linear decodability does not imply behavioral efficacy.
bullets: Omni Models can answer differently to semantically equivalent audio, visual, and textual inputs.
The study separates an Answer Subspace from a representation that predicts whether cross-modal disagreement will occur.
Across three Omni Models and two multimodal reasoning tasks, disagreement-predictive information concentrates in a reproducible two-dimensional representation outside the Answer Subspace.
Perturbing the Answer Subspace changes predictions, while perturbing the disagreement representation has little effect, similar to a matched random subspace.
Applying Answer Subspace perturbations to one modality induces disagreement; applying the same perturbation to both modalities largely preserves agreement.

figures.caption: Figure 6: Paired audio and image representations in the Answer Subspace across six model–task conditions. Gray lines connect the two modality conditions of each item. Agreement pairs remain within the same answer region, whereas disagreement pairs separate across answer regions.

The remaining columns are the fraction of pairs on which the answer decoded from the Answer Subspace agrees with the model’s new prediction, overall and restricted to the two behavior groups. Disagreement items change more often in four of the six conditions, and the sign of that difference agrees with the difference in settling depth — the normalized depth from which the decoded answer stops changing — in every condition (ρ = 0.94, p = 0.005). At α = 40 both cohorts are near ceiling and the difference disappears. Cohort sizes are unequal because the split follows the model’s own behavior, so these comparisons are the least powered in the paper and we do not build any claim in the body on them.

The complement matches the full state to within 0.014 in every condition, while the two rank-matched readouts of the same complement fall well short of it, so the result does not follow from the complement’s dimensionality alone.

A fully answer-pair-matched comparison is impossible because a fixed pair of predictions determines the disagreement label, so we stratify on the audio-condition prediction alone and pool the within-stratum results. The Disagreement-Predictive Subspace and the random control are both near zero and show no consistent ordering: the random control exceeds the disagreement subspace in three of the six conditions, most visibly for Gemma-4-E4B on spatial, where a random two-dimensional subspace changes 18 predictions. In that condition the two arms are therefore not distinguishable and the claim rests on the gap against the Answer Subspace rather than on an ordering between the controls.

Asymmetric perturbs the Answer Subspace under one modality only; the symmetric control applies the identical shift to both. N is the number of originally agreeing items evaluated. The asymmetric arm exceeds the control in all six conditions at α = 40 (by at least a factor of 3.07), in five of six at α = 20, and in none at α ≤ 5.

papers.selection_reason: Representation-subspace analysis of cross-modal inconsistency in omni models, directly relevant to multimodal foundation models.
papers.title: Understanding Cross-Modal Inconsistency through Representation Subspaces in Omni Models
papers.tldr: Cross-modal inconsistency is predicted by a distinct low-dimensional representation, but disagreement is behaviorally induced by misaligning modality-specific answer representations.

papers.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) provide a unified interface for language-conditioned visual perception. In pixel-to-sequence grounding, autoregressive coordinate generation requires multiple sequential decoding steps per box, increasing inference cost with the number of instances. Pixel-to-embedding methods reduce this overhead but lack explicit spatial encoding when using a shared special token. We introduce SemGeo, a token-efficient visual grounding framework that represents each instance with a single grid token for coarse localization. A geometric decoder reuses visual features and hidden states to recover precise discrete box coordinates in parallel. To train proposal generation and box localization together, we introduce Gaussian soft labels that encode coordinate distances during supervised fine-tuning (SFT). Reinforcement post-training further combines box-set rewards with coordinate supervision on model-generated proposals. This stage trains the language model and geometric decoder on their own predictions to mitigate the mismatch between teacher-forced training and inference. Across eight benchmarks spanning object detection, referring object detection, and document layout grounding, SemGeo achieves the highest F1@mIou among compared MLLMs on six benchmarks. It also delivers $2.07\times$ and $1.25\times$ the mean box-generation throughput of representative grounding baselines under vLLM and Transformers, respectively, while achieving higher accuracy in both comparisons.
authors: Zhaojie Chen, Junyan Yang, Le Yang, Qi Dang, Yucheng Huang, Qianyi Che, Zhaoqiang Chen, Xinqi Zhu, Qiang Zhao
bullets: Autoregressive coordinate generation is costly because each box requires multiple sequential decoding steps.
SemGeo uses a single grid token for coarse instance localization, then a geometric decoder recovers precise discrete box coordinates in parallel.
Gaussian soft labels encode coordinate distances to jointly train proposal generation and localization.
Reinforcement post-training uses model-generated proposals with box-set rewards and coordinate supervision to reduce the teacher-forcing mismatch.
Across eight benchmarks, SemGeo leads in F1@mIoU on six and achieves higher accuracy with 2.07× and 1.25× the mean throughput of representative baselines under vLLM and Transformers.

papers.selection_reason: Token-efficient MLLM visual grounding with geometric decoding and explicit spatial coordinate recovery.
papers.title: Semantic-Guided Geometric Decoding for Token-Efficient Visual Grounding
papers.tldr: SemGeo makes visual grounding more efficient by generating one token per object and decoding precise box coordinates in parallel, achieving strong accuracy with higher throughput.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) are widely used as zero-shot image quality assessors, yet their good-vs-poor answers agree only moderately with human opinion. We ask whether these models fail to see quality or fail to say it. Layer-wise probes on five VLMs point to the second: quality is linearly decodable from the vision encoder and still from the last language layer, far better than the answer reveals, and about a hundred labels recover most of it. The loss lies mainly in the final read-out, which partly reads something else: relative to human opinion, it over-rewards colorfulness and under-rewards sharpness on all five models. We test this by intervention: if the read-out is at fault, a closed-form edit of a single last-layer neuron, fitted to many prompts at once, should close the gap and no more. Both hold. Under prompts never used for fitting, the edit recovers 86--100\% of what a ridge head on the last-layer state, fitted under the same prompts, finds beyond the answer on KonIQ. Where that gap is small, it gains little, too little for our transfer criterion on the two largest models; where the head itself is below the answer, it lowers the score; and it works only when written from the middle of the language model on. Unlike unconstrained fine-tuning, the edit leaves perception question answering intact. It does not carry over to yes-or-no or rating questions, and it reverses the good--poor contrast after sentiment-laden sentences. Code will be made available.
authors: Zhuangzi Li, Shilv Cai, Jian Jin, Zhiyi Pan, Haihong Xiao, Weisi Lin
bullets: VLMs encode image quality well internally, yet their good-vs-poor answers align only moderately with human opinion.
Layer-wise probes across five VLMs indicate the main failure is the final read-out, which overweights colorfulness and underweights sharpness.
The method edits a single last-layer neuron using multiple prompts, without unconstrained fine-tuning.
On unseen prompts for KonIQ, the edit recovers 86–100% of the improvement available from a ridge head on the last-layer state.
The edit is prompt- and layer-sensitive: it does not transfer to yes/no or rating questions and can reverse judgments after sentiment-laden sentences.

papers.selection_reason: Analyzes and edits VLM read-out for image quality assessment; relevant to multimodal LLM behavior.
papers.title: Lost in Read-out: Locating the Image Quality Gap in Vision-Language Models with a Closed-Form Edit
papers.tldr: A closed-form edit to the final language read-out substantially recovers VLM image-quality judgments hidden in their representations, but only under specific prompts and layers.

papers.abstract: The ability to generate multimodal reports integrating fluent narratives with faithful visualizations from tabular data, has become a cornerstone capability for modern vision-language models in practical domains such as finance, healthcare, and policy making. However, existing benchmarks are limited by single-modality focus, simplistic metrics, novelty evaluation, and visualization quality. We address these limitations with MM-ReportBench, a multimodal report evaluation benchmark covering 386 tasks across 185 real-world tables. Each task is paired with an expert-curated reference report featuring standardized chapter structures and verifiable key insight points, constructed through a hybrid pipeline of multimodal reports generation based on Monte Carlo Tree Search and rigorous human quality control. For robust evaluation, we design a dual-judge evaluation framework: Text Judge Model assesses textual quality along structural completeness, grounded insight verification with numerical fact-checking against source tables, and novelty analysis that distinguishes genuine analytical discovery from trivial paraphrasing; Visualization Judge Model evaluates generated visualizations across data fidelity, expressiveness, aesthetics, and technical correctness. They also evaluate cross-modal consistency. Extensive experiments on 20 state-of-the-art models reveal critical weaknesses: even the strongest model achieves only 68.9 overall score, with numerical hallucination affecting 38.5% of reports and genuinely novel insights remaining rare. Our ablation studies further demonstrate that single-judge evaluation consistently inflates scores by 8-12 points compared to dual-judge assessment, confirming that rigorous and reliable benchmarking demands multi-faceted, complementary evaluation probes.
bullets: Covers 386 tasks drawn from 185 real-world tables, with expert-curated reports, standardized structures, and verifiable key insights.
Uses dual judges: a text evaluator checks structure, numerical grounding, and novelty, while a visualization evaluator assesses fidelity, expressiveness, aesthetics, and correctness.
Also measures consistency between generated narratives and visualizations.
Evaluation of 20 state-of-the-art models finds persistent weaknesses, including numerical hallucinations and few genuinely novel insights.
Single-judge evaluation overestimates performance by 8–12 points, supporting complementary multi-faceted evaluation.
papers.selection_reason: Benchmark and dual-judge evaluation for multimodal report generation from tables, directly relevant to multimodal LLM capabilities.
papers.title: MM-ReportBench: A Comprehensive Benchmark for Multimodal Report Generation from Tables
papers.tldr: MM-ReportBench is a 386-task benchmark for evaluating whether models can generate faithful, insightful text-and-visualization reports from tables.

papers.abstract: Omnimodal large language models (Omni-LLMs) integrate audio, video, and text for multimodal reasoning, yet remain vulnerable to cross-modal hallucinations, where one modality improperly influences predictions about another. Existing training-free decoding methods mitigate these errors through modality perturbation or relevance-based weighting. However, due to interference from irrelevant modality cues during fusion and difficulty detecting shared errors, these methods may suppress correct unimodal predictions and allow erroneous consensus to persist. To address these limitations, we propose Provenance-Aware Consensus Decoding (PACD), a training-free framework for mitigating cross-modal hallucinations. PACD comprises two complementary paths based on whether the branches reach consensus. For non-consensus cases, Relevance-Guided Candidate Arbitration identifies task-relevant unimodal evidence and selectively arbitrates between predictions using alternative candidates. For consensus cases, Provenance-Based Consensus Recovery leverages the outranking principle to evaluate the consistency and strength of layer-wise modality evidence for alternative answers, selectively resolving erroneous consensus under confidence constraints. Extensive experiments on four Omni-LLMs and five benchmarks across two tasks demonstrate the superiority of PACD. Compared to existing methods, PACD achieves up to 27.6% relative improvement over standard decoding across CMM, AVHBench, and SVHalluc for cross-modal hallucination mitigation, and an average relative improvement of 7.7% over best baseline across OmniVideoBench and FutureOmni for general audio-visual reasoning.
authors: Chang Sun, Yijun Tian, Zhenwei Tang, Yuchen Deng, Yifan Simon Liu, Chenxu Wang, Wei Wang
bullets: Targets hallucinations caused when irrelevant or misleading audio, video, or text cues distort another modality’s prediction.
Uses Relevance-Guided Candidate Arbitration when unimodal branches disagree, selecting task-relevant evidence and alternative answers.

papers.selection_reason: Training-free decoding to mitigate cross-modal hallucinations in Omni-LLMs; directly relevant to multimodal LLM reasoning and video-language understanding.
papers.title: PACD: Provenance-Aware Consensus Decoding for Mitigating Cross-Modal Hallucinations in Omnimodal Large Language Models

papers.abstract: Conventional knowledge distillation can facilitate the propagation of backdoors from teacher models to student models. However, how this risk manifests in On-Policy Distillation (OPD) remains insufficiently studied. OPD has recently emerged as an important post-training paradigm for Vision-Language Models (VLMs). Unlike traditional offline distillation, OPD does not require teacher-generated responses. Instead, it uses the teacher's probability distributions to supervise response trajectories generated online by the student. Since the initial student model typically generates benign responses and receives no explicit supervision from malicious target responses, OPD appears to offer some inherent resistance to backdoor propagation. In this paper, we challenge this intuition and reveal a more subtle risk of visual backdoor propagation in OPD. Through experiments across multiple model families and datasets, together with theoretical analysis, we identify three main findings. First, unlike the relatively gradual propagation observed in traditional offline distillation, backdoors rarely emerge in OPD at low poisoning ratios. However, the attack success rate rapidly approaches 100% once a critical threshold is exceeded. Second, backdoor propagation does not depend on explicit malicious responses. Instead, it is driven by the continuous accumulation of anomalous probability mass assigned by the teacher. Finally, based on these findings, we propose a novel trigger design that enables visual backdoor propagation with zero explicit trigger injection. These findings further reveal an overlooked mechanism of backdoor propagation in OPD and highlight its potential security risks.
authors: Zane Fu, Yanzhao Zheng, Jinze Liu, Ziting Qin, Qianshan Wei, Jihuai Zhu, Yipeng Yu, Baohua Dong, Hangcheng Zhu, Ruohui Huang
bullets: OPD’s apparent resistance to backdoors is challenged because teacher probability distributions can still transmit malicious behavior.
Unlike offline distillation, propagation is rare at low poisoning ratios but rapidly approaches full attack success beyond a critical threshold.
The mechanism is continuous accumulation of anomalous probability mass from the teacher, rather than explicit malicious target responses.
Experiments across multiple model families and datasets, supported by theoretical analysis, identify this overlooked security risk.
A trigger design is proposed that enables propagation with zero explicit trigger injection.

papers.tldr: On-policy distillation can hide visual backdoor propagation until poisoning crosses a threshold, after which attack success rises sharply—even without malicious responses or explicit trigger injection.

papers.abstract: Multimodal post-training has moved from broad instruction tuning toward reinforcement learning for image and video reasoning, where outcome rewards can improve final-answer accuracy. Yet these rewards are assigned to complete generated trajectories, while visual evidence is used only at sparse and uneven positions inside the response. Recent work has begun to make multimodal RL more token-sensitive through grounding signals or external token-level weighting. We ask a more specific question: can the allocation of the same trajectory-level reward be inferred from the model's own multimodal computation, rather than from an auxiliary annotator, perception module, or process label? We propose Gaze-RL, a representation-driven policy optimization method that redistributes completion-level advantage through a latent reward landing field. The field is computed from internal cross-modal geometry and local predictive uncertainty, assigning larger update weight to positions that are both visually anchored and decision-bearing while remaining mean-one, so the total credit of each rollout is preserved and only its positionwise allocation changes. Gaze-RL requires no process supervision, auxiliary perception module, or architectural modification, and improves both Qwen2.5-VL and InternVL3.5 across a broad range of image and video benchmarks.
authors: Lixuan He, Tianzhe Chu, Shulin Tian, Shikang Zheng, Feng Chen, Yi Ma
bullets: Addresses the mismatch between sequence-level rewards and sparse visual evidence in multimodal reasoning.
Infers a latent reward landing field from cross-modal representations and local predictive uncertainty.
Reweights token-level updates toward positions that are both visually anchored and decision-bearing, while preserving total rollout credit.
Requires no process supervision, auxiliary perception module, or architectural changes.
Improves Qwen2.5-VL and InternVL3.5 across a broad range of image and video benchmarks.

papers.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have achieved impressive performance on a wide range of vision-language tasks. However, it remains unclear whether their predictions are grounded in the visual content itself or are largely driven by statistical co-occurrence patterns and commonsense correlations learned from large-scale image-text corpora. Existing vision-language benchmarks predominantly consist of samples that conform to human commonsense, allowing models to achieve strong performance by exploiting dataset priors rather than genuinely understanding image content. To address this limitation, we present ContraSense, a systematically constructed benchmark for evaluating faithful vision-language understanding. ContraSense consists of carefully curated counter-intuitive image-text pairs that deliberately violate common expectations, substantially reducing the effectiveness of statistical biases and requiring models to rely on visual evidence for reasoning. We conduct comprehensive evaluations on a diverse set of representative open- and closed-source MLLMs. The results reveal a substantial performance gap between current MLLMs and humans: even the strongest closed-source model achieves only about 60\% accuracy, compared with 96.04\% for human participants. These findings demonstrate that current MLLMs still struggle with faithful visual understanding and highlight the need for more robust multimodal reasoning grounded in image content. The ContraSense benchmark is publicly available at https://huggingface.co/datasets/LingLin00/ContraSense.
authors: Ling Lin, Heng Su, Xiangzeng Liu, Yang Bai, Congcong Zhu, Jingrun Chen
bullets: Existing vision-language benchmarks may reward statistical co-occurrences because their examples usually match human expectations.
ContraSense uses carefully curated counter-intuitive image–text pairs that require reasoning from visual evidence.
Evaluations cover diverse open- and closed-source multimodal large language models.
The strongest closed-source model reaches about 60% accuracy, versus 96.04% for humans.
The benchmark highlights the need for more visually grounded multimodal reasoning and is publicly available.

figures.caption: Fig. 1: We propose a new benchmark called ContraSense, which is both creative and imaginative. The benchmark consists of 4,698 carefully crafted and manually calibrated high-resolution (1024 × 1024 pixels) text QA pairs. Each image contains at least one counterintuitive scenario designed to assess whether visual-language models can provide accurate responses based on the image content itself without relying on common-sense prior knowledge from the training data. This benchmark provides a unique and powerful tool for studying the robustness and real-world visual understanding capabilities of VLMs.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) have emerged as central foundation models combining multimodal perception with text comprehension. While VLMs are traditionally built via late fusion by continued pre-training an off-the-shelf language model on multimodal (image-text) data, mixing modalities from the start of pre-training (early fusion) has recently gained traction. However, the fundamental trade-offs between these paradigms remain poorly understood, resulting in expensive and heuristic-driven training recipes. In this paper, we systematically analyze the learning dynamics of these multimodal pre-training processes, showing that validation losses during vision-language fusion can be modeled by separating the base learning trajectory, where different data types contribute at distinct rates, from a distribution shift driven by the competition between modalities. We derive a scaling law that unifiedly describes these dynamics, enabling accurate loss predictions across mixture ratios, training steps, and model sizes. Crucially, our law characterizes the trade-off between early and late fusion: under a fixed data budget, early fusion preserves text performance while late fusion favors vision performance, yielding a trade-off that increasingly tilts toward early fusion as model size scales. Extensive experiments confirm that our scaling law reliably captures multimodal learning dynamics and governs fusion decisions.
authors: Seng Pei Liew, Teppei Suzuki, Seiya Tokui
bullets: Analyzes the trade-offs between early fusion, which mixes modalities from the start, and late fusion, which adapts a pre-trained language model.
Separates learning trajectories by data type from modality competition-induced distribution shifts.
Predicts validation losses across mixture ratios, training steps, and model sizes.
Finds that early fusion better preserves text performance, while late fusion favors vision performance under a fixed data budget.
The trade-off increasingly favors early fusion as model size grows, with experiments supporting the law’s predictive accuracy.

papers.abstract: Identity matching asks whether two records denote the same identity, yet the answer depends on the target granularity. Two records may match at the base level but not at the variant level: they share an underlying design while differing in attributes such as color or size. Final matching accuracy does not separately characterize the capabilities involved. To study this problem, we use e-commerce as a challenging real-world domain. We introduce PURE, a diagnostic benchmark for multi-granularity multimodal identity matching covering four capability dimensions: Perception, Understanding, Reasoning, and Evidence-grounded Judgment. The benchmark comprises 1,457 multiple-choice questions across 14 tasks, derived from real-world matching pairs and verified by two domain experts. Across ten recent MLLMs, overall scores range from 47.1% to 86.0%. Understanding receives the highest mean score and Judgment the lowest, with weaknesses in visual difference localization and variant-level rule judgment. Modality ablations show that models benefit from multimodal evidence but can incorrectly identify conflicts between matching records. In direct matching, most models recognize matching pairs more reliably than non-matching pairs at the base level, whereas the reverse holds at the variant level. PURE therefore reveals what aggregate matching accuracy hides: not only whether models judge a pair correctly, but where they struggle to interpret evidence and apply matching criteria.

papers.abstract: A visual question answering (VQA) model can pass every image-only and question-only test yet fail when the same changes occur together. Standard robustness reports average over conditions and therefore cannot say which accepted requests remain vulnerable. We introduce M3-Test, a coverage audit that aligns each clean input with its single-modality variants and a complete 5x5 family, 4x4 strength joint library, so that any reduced test suite can be replayed on the same requests. Across 2.6 million responses from four vision-language models, joint failures affect 26-29% of the Qwen questions that pass all 40 single-modality tests, although fewer than 0.6% of their joint records fail. Passing the 25 maximum-strength corners does not close this gap: 11-14% of the accepted questions still fail elsewhere in the library. Re-executing the archived failures reproduces about 90% of them, against a 0.3-0.6% flip rate among matched passing controls, and re-checking the most fragile failure records supports 80-89% of them. On the evidence examined, neither execution noise nor grading error can fully account for the gap. The same aligned grids make previous evaluations reusable. On held-out images, a risk order learned from other models discovers about 80% of affected Qwen questions within 25 additional queries, compared with 65-68% for maximum-first and 53-57% for pairwise covering arrays. M3-Test thus turns a passing robustness suite into a request-level account of what remains untested, supporting acceptance, regression review and test allocation.
bullets: VQA models can pass all image-only and question-only tests yet fail when both modalities are perturbed together.
M3-Test aligns each clean request with single-modality variants and a complete 5×5, 4×4-strength joint perturbation library.
Across four vision-language models, 26–29% of Qwen questions passing 40 single-modality tests still had joint failures; maximum-strength corners missed 11–14%.
Archived failures were reproduced at about 90%, while matched passing controls flipped only 0.3–0.6%, suggesting noise and grading errors do not explain the gap.
A cross-model risk order found about 80% of affected Qwen questions within 25 extra queries, outperforming maximum-first and pairwise covering-array strategies.

papers.abstract: Synthetic aperture radar (SAR) foundation models provide transferable representations for diverse perception tasks in all-weather Earth observation. However, their development often relies on costly large-scale SAR pretraining, raising the question of whether such extensive domain-specific pretraining is necessary. We find that modern multimodal large language models (MLLMs) already provide visual encoders that can outperform dedicated SAR foundation models as downstream initializations. This motivates a new paradigm: reuse general visual capabilities and devote domain training to brief specialization. We therefore introduce SARVIA, an adaptive post-pretraining method that specializes modern MLLMs using self-supervised visual questions with computable answers. These questions are constructed from unlabeled observations through general image tasks that capture spatial relations and SAR-specific tasks that exploit native measurements and SAR--optical correspondence. A shared answer-prediction objective jointly trains low-rank adapters across visual and language components, with loss-driven task sampling. We then export the adapted visual encoder as a standalone backbone. With 600 adaptation steps and 2 GPU-hours, SARVIA outperforms the compared foundation models on all six SAR detection and segmentation benchmarks. Compared with dedicated SAR pretraining, SARVIA reduces domain-training costs by orders of magnitude while improving visual transfer across architectures and scales. This new paradigm shifts the emphasis from repeated, costly pretraining to a reusable specialization process that can benefit from advances in open MLLMs. Dataset and code: https://github.com/zcablii/SARVIA.
authors: Yuxuan Li, Zichen Tian, Qianru Sun
bullets: Motivation: Large-scale SAR-specific pretraining is costly, and modern MLLM visual encoders can provide strong downstream initializations.
Method: Adapt MLLMs with self-supervised visual questions derived from unlabeled imagery, combining general spatial tasks with SAR-specific measurements and SAR–optical correspondence.
Optimization: Jointly train low-rank adapters across visual and language components using a shared answer-prediction objective and loss-driven task sampling.
Result: Using 600 adaptation steps and 2 GPU-hours, SARVIA outperforms the compared foundation models across six SAR detection and segmentation benchmarks.
Scope: The adapted visual encoder is exported as a standalone backbone, emphasizing reusable specialization rather than repeated SAR pretraining.

papers.abstract: Decision models can answer a typed question about an image with a probability per option, without generating text. In our case study of Clef-flash (post-trained Qwen3.5-9B backbone) on industrial inspection benchmarks, we ask whether it localizes the anomalies it detects. We obtained uneven results with zero-shot detection: per-category image AUROC 0.924 on MVTec AD and 0.668 on MVTec AD 2. On the former, the decision head's routing attention produces 0.391 mean per-image pixel AUROC, and hiding the image tokens from it leaves detection unchanged. The multimodal LLM's backbone attention does point at the defect, however it falls below a center prior when we change question. It falls below chance if we remove textual context in the question, partly due to backbone attention leaving the object, while the head's map hardly changes. The backbone's states carry the location when probed with normal images, on the test-split images, however, the decision depends on the defect region. A larger model, Clef, that comes with a post-trained Qwen3.8-27B backbone, gives no useful map in the decision head either. We found that it's possible to recover anomaly location by asking question specifically on an image region, retraining the head or reading the backbone, but none matches dedicated few-shot localizers.
bullets: Zero-shot image-level detection is strong on MVTec AD but weaker on MVTec AD 2.
The decision head’s routing attention provides poor pixel localization, and hiding image tokens does not change detection.
Backbone attention can indicate defects, but localization depends on question wording and textual context and may fall below chance.
Anomaly location can be recovered through region-specific questions, head retraining, or backbone probing, though none matches dedicated few-shot localizers.
A larger Clef model also produces no useful localization map in its decision head.
papers.selection_reason: Case study of a Qwen-based multimodal decision model and its anomaly localization is relevant to multimodal LLM behavior.
papers.title: Deciding Without Pointing: A Case Study of Whether a Decision Model Localizes the Anomalies It Detects
papers.tldr: Clef-flash detects industrial image anomalies but its decision head generally does not reliably localize them.

papers.abstract: Bird's-Eye-View (BEV)-conditioned large language models (LLMs) enable language-interactive driving, but onboard deployment requires efficient perception and continuous planning alongside autoregressive language generation. We present GridDriver, an efficient BEV-conditioned LLM framework combining trajectory prediction, structured driving indicators, natural-language navigation, driving explanations, and scene question answering. Lightweight spatio-temporal BEV perception and spatially structured tokens provide scene context to a shared LLM, while frame-wise scheduling interleaves trajectory prediction with asynchronous language generation. GridDriver achieves competitive performance on public benchmarks, reaching 87.9% PDMS on NAVSIM and 57.6% accuracy on nuScenes-QA with a shared planning and QA checkpoint. Spatial representation analyses demonstrate improved geometric information retention and trajectory prediction compared with Q-Former compression. The system achieves 32.7 ms standalone planning latency and 9.4 plans/s in an onboard ROS 2 pipeline. We further evaluate planning on our own data recordings and demonstrate open-loop onboard operation on a research vehicle. Across public benchmarks and real-world evaluations, we identify strengths and limitations of the BEV-based approach.
authors: Katharina Winter, William Engel, Zain A. Alishammat, Fabian B. Flohr
bullets: Addresses the challenge of running autoregressive language generation alongside real-time onboard driving planning.
Uses lightweight spatio-temporal BEV perception, spatially structured tokens, and frame-wise scheduling to interleave planning with asynchronous language generation.
Supports trajectory prediction, structured driving indicators, navigation instructions, driving explanations, and scene question answering.
Reports 87.9% PDMS on NAVSIM, 57.6% nuScenes-QA accuracy, 32.7 ms standalone planning latency, and 9.4 plans/s in an onboard ROS 2 pipeline.
Evaluations include public benchmarks, proprietary recordings, and open-loop operation on a research vehicle; the abstract notes both strengths and limitations of the BEV-based approach.

papers.abstract: Speculative decoding accelerates vision-language models(VLMs) while preserving the target model's outputs, but its speedup diminishes under high concurrency serving as the system becomes more compute bounded as the batch size increases. This problem is pronounced for multimodal speculative decoding as the long range of the image tokens in the prompt can significantly increase the computational cost during draft token prediction. The block-diffusion drafters (e.g. DFlash, DSpark) can effectively speed up the draft model efficiency by predicting multiple draft tokens in one forward pass, but their speedup for VLMs under high concurrency is still modest (<9%). In order to understand this gap, we examine the information flow between different modalities from target model to draft model and identify the sparsity pattern of visual attention between the target and draft models: only small set of key-value heads in the draft model need direct visual feature attention in the context and only visual features from top level layers in the target model need to be attended in the context. We therefore propose VisHead-Spec, which selects a small, fixed set of key-value (KV) heads to attend to all image features from top level layers in the target model and restricts the remaining heads to text features. On Qwen3-VL-8B and MMSpec, VisHead-Spec-8 lets 8 of the drafter's 40 KV heads read the image while keeping accepted length within 0.3% of the block-diffusion draft model baseline (i.e. DSpark). At batch size 64, its throughput gain over autoregressive decoding increases to 16.0%, compared with 9.5% for DSpark; at batch size 1, its speedup remains comparable to DSpark.
authors: Xin Guo, Arushi Rai, Xiang Zhou, Qiang Zhang, Siyu Lin, Xiangjun Fan, Lizhu Zhang
bullets: High-concurrency VLM serving becomes compute-bound, while long image-token contexts make draft prediction expensive.
The method identifies sparse cross-modal information flow: only a few draft KV heads need visual features, primarily from the target model’s top layers.
VisHead-Spec-8 routes image features to 8 of 40 KV heads and restricts the rest to text features.
On Qwen3-VL-8B and MMSpec, accepted length stays within 0.3% of the DSpark baseline.
At batch size 64, throughput gain reaches 16.0% versus 9.5% for DSpark; at batch size 1, performance remains comparable.

papers.title: VisHead-Spec: Head-Routed Visual Attention for Multimodal Speculative Decoding
papers.tldr: VisHead-Spec accelerates multimodal speculative decoding under high concurrency by routing visual attention through only a small subset of draft-model KV heads.

papers.abstract: Multimodal models increasingly reason by synthesizing pixels, sketching maze paths within interleaved chains of thought or rolling out video solutions frame by frame. Each visual thought runs the full diffusion schedule inherited from photorealistic synthesis, so iterative denoising dominates inference cost. We study how to allocate test-time compute along two axes: when to render visual thoughts rather than thinking in text or answering directly, and how many denoising steps each thought requires. Controlled interventions that vary only how the thought is rendered uncover three regimes. Causal thoughts carry the plan and become legible early: an 8-step sketch nearly matches a 50-step render in accuracy, commits to the same plan as often as two independent full renders agree, and in video models mostly fails by stalling short of the goal, so the rollout abstains. Decorative thoughts can be omitted without loss, whereas harmful thoughts lower accuracy. Because the regime depends on both model and task, always drawing is suboptimal. Across 14 model-benchmark pairs of three interleaved reasoners, answering directly, without any thinking, wins 9 pairs, and choosing among direct, text-only, and visual tiers from ten labeled examples per pair raises mean accuracy from 60.7% (always drawing) to 65.1%. Where drawing pays, we propose sketch-and-vote, which samples 8-step sketches (a step count chosen without labels) from independent noises until one answer reaches three votes. With this one setting, sketch-and-vote beats full rendering with fewer denoising steps on an image reasoner and two video reasoners, by 8.6 points on VSP spatial planning and by 9.6 and 22.1 points on mazes.
authors: Sheng Lu, Guangpin Tao, Tong Lu, Ying Tai
bullets: Full diffusion denoising makes visual thoughts expensive, but causal plans often become clear after only 8 steps.
Visual thoughts vary by role: causal sketches help, decorative thoughts can be omitted, and harmful thoughts may reduce accuracy.
Across 14 model–benchmark pairs, direct answering was best in 9; selecting among direct, text-only, and visual modes improved mean accuracy from 60.7% to 65.1%.
The proposed sketch-and-vote method samples 8-step sketches until one answer gets three votes, outperforming full rendering on selected image and video reasoning tasks.
The best rendering strategy depends on both the model and task; video rollouts may fail by stalling before reaching the goal and should abstain.
