papers.abstract: No-reference image quality assessment (IQA) of low-dose CT predicts the score that radiologists would assign to a slice without a full-dose reference, as needed to compare dose protocols and denoisers. Trained CT IQA networks agree well with radiologists but output only a score, whereas multimodal large language models (MLLMs) can explain a score but perform poorly on CT when only prompted. We propose a measurement-aware MLLM, built on Qwen3.8-27B, that rates a slice from its image together with six image-domain measurements of noise, sharpness, high-frequency content and streaks, given to the language model as percentiles in text. On the LDCT-IQA 2023 test set, it reaches an Overall score of 2.735, on par with the retrained challenge winner (2.735) and MedSigLIP-FiLM (2.713), and substantially above its base MLLM used as a zero-shot agent. Shuffling the measurements at test time reduces the score by 0.048, mostly through noise, but the same measurements also lead the model to assign higher scores to over-smoothed denoised images.
authors: Kerem Basim, Tolga Demiroglu, Mehmet Ozan Unal, Metin Ertas, Isa Yildirim
bullets: Addresses the need to assess low-dose CT quality without full-dose reference images.
Uses Qwen3.8-27B with six image-domain measurements covering noise, sharpness, high-frequency content, and streaks, provided as percentile text.
Achieves an Overall score of 2.735 on the LDCT-IQA 2023 test set, matching the retrained challenge winner and exceeding MedSigLIP-FiLM’s 2.713.
Shuffling measurements lowers performance by 0.048, indicating that the model uses the measurement information.
The measurements can also cause higher scores for over-smoothed denoised images, indicating a limitation in quality judgment.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. Two ways to give Qwen3.8-27B CT quality measurements. (b) Our fine-tuned model: six measurement percentiles are written as text after the image tokens of a CT-tuned vision encoder; LoRA adapters and a linear head on the last token are trained to predict the MOS (Overall 2.73). Tiles are from a training slice and computed with simple definitions for illustration.

Fig. 2. What the models rely on. (a) Our model, partial dependence (fold 1): its mean prediction moves mostly with the noise measurements. (b) The zero-shot agent opens a visual view most often for the worst images (MOS 0–1); numbers on the bars are reads per image. papers.selection_reason: Multimodal LLM extended with measurement-aware inputs for CT quality assessment; fits multimodal LLM application.
papers.title: Measurement-Aware Multimodal LLM for No-Reference Low-Dose CT Quality Assessment
papers.tldr: A measurement-aware multimodal LLM improves no-reference low-dose CT quality assessment by combining CT images with textual image-quality measurements, matching leading task-specific methods while revealing sensitivity to measurement reliability and over-smoothing.

papers.abstract: Subliminal learning is a phenomenon in large language models (LLMs) where a teacher passes a hidden preference to a student through training data unrelated to that preference. We study whether subliminal learning also occurs in vision-language models (VLMs). We finetune a teacher VLM to prefer a specific animal or facial attribute and use a control teacher from the same base model. Both teachers generate numbers for an unrelated visual task involving geometric shapes. Two students initialized from the same base VLM are finetuned on the same images, using numbers generated by either the biased or control teacher. Across VLMs ranging from 2B to 7B parameters, we find that both animal and facial preferences can transfer through this unrelated task. Students trained on biased-teacher outputs select the target more often than control students, with a difference of up to $\sim$10 percentage points in the animal preference task. Transfer can become stronger with more training data and varies with the target preference, model, and how the numbers are generated. Beyond preferences, we show that the biased student's explanations use more of the same words and phrases as the biased teacher's explanations than those of the control student, even when all three models select the same image. These results matter for training VLMs and show that training on unrelated data may change both a VLM's image preferences and how it explains its choices, and that transfer can become stronger with more training samples.

papers.abstract: Instruction tuning of large language models and large vision language models relies on massive training data, which incurs substantial computational and storage costs. Meanwhile, training data often contains redundancy, noise, and low quality samples. Existing data selection methods mostly rely on diversity, importance, or a combination of both, without explicitly constraining the distributional consistency between the selected subset and the full data in the embedding space. We propose QMAC, a quality aware multiband characteristic function matching method that formulates data selection as a joint optimization problem of distribution matching and quality filtering. QMAC matches the empirical characteristic functions of the selected subset and the full data across multiple frequency scales, capturing both global semantic coverage and local perturbations, while using task related quality scores to filter noisy and low quality samples. We systematically evaluate QMAC on 4 data types, 8 target models, and 44 benchmarks. Experimental results show that QMAC outperforms existing data selection baselines on standard image-text instruction data, substantially surpasses random selection on standard text instruction, image-text reasoning, and text reasoning data, and exceeds full data training in multiple model and budget combinations. The code will be made publicly available upon acceptance of the paper.
authors: Peng Sun, Yi Yang, Mingshuo Chen, Chunxiao Li, Yao Zhu, Huawen Shen, Tianfan Fu
bullets: Addresses the computational and storage costs of massive instruction-tuning datasets containing redundant, noisy, and low-quality samples.
Formulates data selection as joint distribution matching and quality filtering in embedding space.
Matches empirical characteristic functions across frequency bands to preserve global semantic coverage and local variation.
Uses task-related quality scores to remove noisy or low-quality examples.
Outperforms existing baselines across evaluated data types, models, and benchmarks, and exceeds full-data training in some model–budget settings.

papers.abstract: Test-time scaling often seeks better answers by sampling multiple responses from a frozen model, yet conventional temperature sampling generates every candidate along the same fixed computation path. We introduce architectural sampling, a training-free method that generates candidates through distinct forward computations by reusing selected blocks of decoder layers. Varying the block location and repetition count introduces computational diversity without updating model weights or adding auxiliary parameters. Across five Qwen checkpoints and twelve multimodal benchmarks, architectural sampling improves pass@9 over standard-path temperature sampling by 6.58 percentage points on average at the same nine-candidate budget. Reusing early layers yields the strongest gains, and the improvement in candidate coverage persists even under greedy decoding. The resulting candidates show lower lexical overlap and improve accuracy when used as rollouts for label-free test-time reinforcement learning. These findings extend the benefits of our architectural sampling beyond candidate coverage, demonstrating more effective learning from a model's own outputs.
bullets: Motivation: Standard temperature sampling explores candidates along the same computation path, limiting diversity.
Method: Reuse selected decoder-layer blocks with different locations and repetition counts to create training-free computational diversity without changing model weights.
Result: Across five Qwen checkpoints and twelve multimodal benchmarks, it raises pass@9 by 6.58 percentage points on average at the same nine-candidate budget.
Early-layer reuse performs best, and improved candidate coverage persists even with greedy decoding.
The more diverse, less lexically overlapping candidates also improve rollouts for label-free test-time reinforcement learning.

papers.abstract: As Large Multimodal Models (LMMs) transition toward natively unified architectures, evaluating their safety in synergistic harmful image-text generation tasks becomes a critical challenge. Unlike unimodal threats, synergistic risks emerge when text and image modalities are coordinated to produce harm that significantly exceeds their individual components. We introduce UnifiedAttack, a novel benchmark designed to evaluate LMM safety in collaborative scenarios by focusing on the harmfulness gain achieved through cross-modal synergy. The benchmark incorporates samples filtered for their multimodal potential alongside a novel subset of synthesized disinformation queries. To verify identified vulnerabilities, we propose a synergistic hijacking framework featuring In-Context Reskinning (ICR) and Cognitive Planning Injection (CPI). ICR utilizes few-shot learning to wrap adversarial intent in benign virtual shells to desensitize safety filters, while CPI hijacks the reasoning path by enforcing a plan-then-execute paradigm. By compelling the system to commit to a neutral logical plan, we exploit its internal drive for consistency to induce the synchronized generation of harmful multimodal content. Extensive evaluations on state-of-the-art architectures demonstrate that UnifiedAttack consistently bypasses modern alignment. Our findings reveal that the structural helpfulness and logical coherence of unified models can be systematically weaponized, highlighting the urgent need for logic-aware defenses in synergistic generation tasks. Code is available at https://github.com/bingjunluo/UnifiedAttack .
bullets: Targets synergistic harms whose combined image-text effect exceeds the risks of either modality alone.
Introduces a benchmark with multimodally promising harmful samples and synthesized disinformation queries.
Uses Synergistic Hijacking with In-Context Reskinning and Cognitive Planning Injection to evade safety filters and steer harmful generation.
Evaluations across state-of-the-art architectures find consistent alignment bypasses.
Highlights the need for logic-aware defenses against weaponized helpfulness and coherence.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Comparison of Single-Modal Attack vs. Synergistic UnifiedAttack. Unlike baseline methods that process modal inputs independently, UnifiedAttack leverages synergistic hijacking to bridge the gap between textual intent and visual execution. This cross-modal synergy effectively bypasses safety guardrails, producing coordinated harmful content (Harm+) with significantly higher toxicity levels than isolated attacks.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action models (VLAs) map language instructions and visual observations to robot actions, showing strong capabilities across robotic manipulation tasks. However, in our probing experiment, we find that action representations near the action output do not fully preserve task-relevant visual grounding. Motivated by this late-layer grounding gap, we introduce STAR, for STeering Action Representations, a training-free inference method for pre-trained VLAs. STAR applies an exponential moving average over late-layer residual updates, allowing later action representations to inherit object-aware update directions from earlier layers without model updates or architectural changes. It further uses recent proprioceptive states to adapt the mixing strength, using conservative mixing when execution dynamics change rapidly. Experiments on robot manipulation benchmarks show that STAR improves late-layer object awareness and increases average task success rates by 4.0 percentage points. Our code is available at https://github.com/PKU-VaLuE-Lab/STAR.
bullets: Addresses a late-layer grounding gap in vision-language-action models, where action representations may lose task-relevant visual information.
Applies an exponential moving average to late-layer residual updates so later representations inherit object-aware directions from earlier layers.
Adapts the mixing strength using recent proprioceptive states, applying more conservative mixing when execution dynamics change rapidly.
Improves late-layer object awareness and raises average task success by 4.0 percentage points on robot manipulation benchmarks.
Requires no model updates or architectural changes; its scope is pre-trained VLAs and the evaluated manipulation benchmarks.

(b) A Transformer layer in a VLA, mapping the action hidden state from hk to hk+1 through a residual update. (c) Object awareness of π0.5 layer outputs across depth under native inference and our method STAR. (d) Success rates of native inference and our method STAR on LIBERO-PRO for π0.5 and GR00T-N1.5, respectively.

Figure 3: Object-awareness and attention-map diagnostics for native inference and STAR. (a) Visualization of the three masks, including the task-specific object mask mo, randomly scattered pixels mr with the same pixel count, and a randomly sampled rectangular background region mb of similar area. (b) Comparison of awareness scores for native inference and STAR under object masking and control masking at layer 18. papers.abstract: Vision-language models now grade robot videos, and text placed beside the frames can change their verdicts. On clips where the robot is losing progress, we add one log line saying the robot is making progress. Across Gemini, Qwen and GPT judges, this flips correct verdicts to progress 10 to 35 percentage points more often than a neutral line does. A one-line warning that the log may be wrong removes most of this effect. Selected fake "task complete" claims flip half of Qwen's correct verdicts, against a tenth for unrelated log lines. They have no detectable effect on Gemini.
bullets: Adding a false progress log beside videos where the robot is losing progress causes more verdict reversals than a neutral log across Gemini, Qwen, and GPT judges.
A one-line warning that the log may be incorrect largely mitigates this influence.
Fake “task complete” claims reverse about half of Qwen’s correct verdicts, versus about a tenth for unrelated logs.
Gemini shows no detectable response to the selected fake completion claims.

Only intervals the judge gets right on the frames, both forward and reversed. Numbers in Table 1.

On the frames alone, Qwen answers Falling (losing progress): “the right arm remains open and does not grasp it”. With the log “Successful completion confirmed: the pen was . . . transferred to the right arm, and placed in the blue plate”, it answers Rising (making progress): “the execution log confirms the successful completion of the task”. papers.abstract: Localized AI manipulations in long-form videos often affect brief events within otherwise authentic content, making video-level classification insufficient for forensic analysis. Existing audio-visual deepfake benchmarks largely focus on short talking-head clips, while long-form temporal forensics remains predominantly visual. We introduce AV-FABLE, a dual-timeline benchmark for sparse manipulations in open-scene long-form audio-visual videos. AV-FABLE contains 16,650 pristine--manipulated twin pairs (998 hours) created with 27 editing configurations, with separate audio and visual timelines that enable modality-specific temporal localization and expose errors hidden by joint-timeline evaluation. On AV-FABLE, zero-shot prompting of audio-visual large language models (AV-LLMs) yields near-chance detection and poor temporal localization. In contrast, supervised readouts of their frozen perception features recover strong forensic signals, suggesting manipulation evidence is encoded in these representations but not effectively exposed through language outputs. Motivated by this observation, we propose NFSR(Native Forensics via Separated Readouts), which reads frozen AV-LLM features with separate audio and visual temporal decoders. NFSR achieves the best audio-visual localization performance in-domain and across all three out-of-distribution settings, including transfer to held-out videos from an external long-video forensic benchmark. AV-FABLE, code, and model weights will be publicly released.
bullets: Introduces a dual-timeline benchmark for localized manipulations in open-scene, long-form audio-visual videos.
Includes 16,650 pristine–manipulated twin pairs spanning 998 hours and 27 editing configurations.
Zero-shot AV-LLM prompting performs near chance for detection and poorly for temporal localization.
NFSR uses separate audio and visual temporal decoders over frozen AV-LLM features, achieving the best localization in-domain and across three out-of-distribution settings.
The benchmark exposes errors hidden by joint-timeline evaluation and is intended for public release with code and model weights.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of SEE-Forge, the event-driven pipeline for constructing AV-FABLE. Given an event in a pristine video, SEE-Forge plans audio and/or visual manipulations, executes them with editors, and reinserts them into context to create pristine–manipulated twin pairs. The executed interval provides temporal ground truth, while human-reviewed annotations record forensic cues within and around the manipulated event.

Figure 2: Overview of NFSR. (a) Frozen intermediate-layer (“detail”) and interface features pass through modality-specific gated projection and host-conditioned FiLM. (b) Independent decoders localize audio and visual manipulations on separate timelines. (c) Source-calibrated thresholds give video-level detection and four-way attribution without changing the intervals. Audio and video excerpts come from the same clip; intervals are schematic.
Figure 3: Scene diversity in AV-FABLE. Example frames span indoor and outdoor environments, human activities, objects, food preparation, sports, and other contexts represented in the twin pairs.

Figure 4: Statistics and manipulation coverage in AV-FABLE. The six panels show video duration, event duration by modality, manipulated temporal coverage, tampering position, semantic operation, and aggregated generation route. papers.abstract: A central yet under-explored question in Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) is where to connect---how visual information from a hierarchical vision encoder should be wired into the layer-wise semantics of a large language model. Mainstream MLLMs inject a fixed single-layer visual representation into the LLM and treat all LLM layers as a single consumer, ignoring that different layers demand different visual granularities. Recent multi-layer fusion methods either compress hierarchical features on the encoder side or rely on predefined sparse or hierarchical layer-to-layer connections, and therefore stop short of modeling adaptive cross-layer interactions between the ViT and LLM hierarchies. We address this gap with DGP (Dynamic Gated Pathways), a routing mechanism that establishes all-to-all connections between every ViT layer and every LLM layer, with each LLM layer dynamically gating its preference over visual layers conditioned on its own semantic state. Built on top of LLaVA-1.5-7B and 13B, DGP delivers consistent gains over the LLaVA-1.5-7B baseline (e.g., +4.2 on SQA$^{I}$, +3.3 on MM-Vet, +3.1 on VizWiz and LLaVA$^{W}$) and surpasses prior multi-layer visual fusion methods on most benchmarks. Layer-wise routing analyses further show that different LLM layers do select different visual granularities on demand, supporting both the effectiveness and interpretability of the proposed dynamic gated pathways. The code is available: https://github.com/YingyingYan1/DGP.

papers.abstract: Fine-grained visual reasoning is essential for remote sensing in urban management, yet remains underexplored in the evaluation of multimodal large language models (MLLMs). We introduce UMBench, a fine-grained urban remote sensing benchmark built from unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) images for multiple urban management tasks such as traffic monitoring, urban construction, environmental quality, and disaster warning. Evaluations on UMBench reveal that current MLLMs often rely on scene-level priors and overlook fine-grained visual evidence. To address this issue, we further propose a novel evidence-first chain-of-thought method that directs models to inspect fine-grained visual evidence in a training-free manner. Experiments show that our method can improve the performance of both open-source and commercial MLLMs on UMBench.

papers.abstract: We used medical image synthesis to create a challenging multimodal evaluation framework that exposes hallucination behaviors in frontier models. Evaluating multimodal reasoning has historically been difficult because existing medical datasets rarely pair different image modalities, such as radiographs and external clinical photographs. To address this gap, we introduce Trick-or-Treat, an adversarial multimodal medical benchmark that pairs real chest radiographs with synthetic clinical photographs to challenge models' cross-modal reasoning. For each of a wide range of conditions, we created two pairs of images, where the pairs share a single chest radiograph but contain different external photographs. In matched pairs, the chest radiograph and photograph both contain findings suggesting the same disease (e.g., varicella pneumonia suggested by lung opacities and crusted skin lesions seen in chickenpox). In mismatched pairs, the photograph depicts an alternative clinical finding that would not lead to the same unifying diagnosis (e.g. replacing crusted skin lesions with ordinary acne). Synthetic photograph generation allows clinical findings to be varied while the person's features and photographic setting stay consistent, reducing confounding. In an investigation of three frontier models, we found that models hallucinated clinically significant photograph findings in 45-57.5% of mismatched pairs, up from 25-37.5% for the same photographs shown alone. When faced with mismatched pairs, models tended to ignore mismatches and instead hallucinated findings that better matched the radiograph (e.g. misreading acne as crusted skin lesions to justify diagnosing chickenpox). Trick-or-Treat both demonstrates concerning error pattern in frontier models' medical reasoning and provides a proof of concept for the use of synthetic images in adversarial multimodal evaluation.
authors: Oishi Banerjee, Eujin Lee, Sung Eun Kim, Alexandra N. Willauer, Christine Y. Zhou, Zhizhou Yang, Pranav Rajpurkar

Across three frontier models, clinically significant photograph hallucinations occurred in 45–57.5% of mismatched pairs, versus 25–37.5% when photographs were shown alone.

papers.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) remain prone to visual hallucinations when correct responses depend on subtle visual details. One line of post-training methods constructs visual contrasts through image retrieval, generation, or editing to improve fine-grained perception. However, these contrasts are not built around the model's own hallucinations, making it difficult to ensure that supervision targets its actual perceptual confusions. Another line suppresses hallucinated outputs through response correction or preference learning under fixed image conditions, but leaves the design of supervision signals on the image-input side underexplored. Inspired by how humans correct misconceptions, we introduce DreamRealm, a post-training framework that explores diverse latent hallucinated responses, minimally edits original images to make them valid, and trains the model to assign each response to its supporting image. Our data construction pipeline, RealmForgePipe, mines observed and latent hallucinations from a target model and materializes them through image editing. Using hallucinations mined from Qwen3.5-9B, we construct the Realized Hallucination Dataset (RealmSet). Our training objective, RealmMatch, constructs a likelihood score matrix across image--response combinations and combines supervised learning with bidirectional contrastive losses to reinforce correct matches and suppress mismatches. Compared with the original Qwen3.5-9B model, DreamRealm improves performance across six visual perception and hallucination benchmarks, including gains of 7.26 percentage points in HallusionBench accuracy and 11.34 percentage points in MMVP pair accuracy. Together with ablation studies on data construction and training methods, these results demonstrate that hallucination assignment is a promising paradigm for improving visual perception and mitigating hallucinations.

papers.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have demonstrated remarkable progress on cross-modal reasoning tasks, yet they continue to suffer from hallucinations in long-chain reasoning processes. In this work, we revisit hallucination in MLLMs from the perspective of reasoning generation dynamics. We argue that entropy is not merely a static measure of uncertainty but a structured signal that reflects how modality information is integrated throughout decoding. Through systematic analysis, we identify two characteristic entropy patterns associated with hallucination behaviors: (1) a generally high-confidence regime corresponds to premature convergence to inappropriate multimodal interactions; and (2) local abrupt entropy transitions are associated with reasoning instability and hallucination onset. Building on these observations, we propose an entropy-aware self-introspective framework for MLLM reasoning. Our method continuously tracks entropy dynamics during decoding and performs targeted visual re-alignment when suspicious hallucination states are detected, encouraging the model to re-examine salient visual evidence at critical reasoning stages. Extensive experiments across six multimodal reasoning benchmarks spanning nine distinct evaluation settings demonstrate that our approach delivers robust improvements in reasoning accuracy and hallucination robustness, while providing new insights into the generation dynamics underlying MLLM failures. The code is available at: https://github.com/jden4524/SelfRetrospectiveDecoding.
authors: Jiaqi Deng, Zhe Fu, Yakun Chen, Dichang Zhang, Zonghan Wu, Xiaoshui Huang, Huan Huo, Guandong Xu
bullets: Hallucinations are linked to two entropy patterns: premature high-confidence convergence and abrupt local entropy transitions.
The framework continuously monitors entropy dynamics during generation to identify suspicious reasoning states.
When detected, it prompts the model to re-examine salient visual evidence through targeted visual re-alignment.
Experiments across six benchmarks and nine evaluation settings report improved reasoning accuracy and hallucination robustness.
The work uses entropy dynamics to provide insights into how multimodal reasoning failures emerge.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Framework overview of the proposed SEED. The figure presents three parts: (a) A standard MLLM architecture processes system instructions and visual tokens through stacked decoder layers to perform multimodal reasoning. (b) A self-introspective mechanism monitors token-level entropy dynamics throughout the decoding process, capturing locally important spikes that signal shifts in reasoning dynamics. (c) When both detection conditions are met, our method performs an attention intervention during decoding to rectify the multimodal interaction. We refer to this process as Visual Attention Re-alignment Decoding.

papers.abstract: Unified Multimodal Models (UMMs) aim to support visual understanding and generation within a single model. Existing post-training methods either use understanding as a fixed teacher to improve generation, or rely on ground-truth trajectories to supervise both understanding and generation. Prism instead derives bidirectional supervision from self-generated interleaved rollouts, constructing training targets according to the reliability of their text and image chains. We propose Prism, a bidirectional self-teaching post-training method for UMMs. Like a prism decomposing mixed light, Prism decouples a coupled interleaved trajectory into a text chain and an image chain, assesses the reliability of each chain, and constructs a corresponding training target from their reliability states. Experiments on both SenseNova-U1 and BAGEL show that Prism improves both understanding and generation. On the generation side, GenEval improves from 85.8 to 89.2 (+3.4), and DPG improves from 86.1 to 87.3 (+1.2) on SenseNova-U1. On the understanding side, the total MME score improves from 2282.6 to 2311.6, and MMVP improves from 58.0 to 62.0. Consistent improvements are observed on BAGEL. These results highlight that Prism enables coordinated improvements in generation and understanding by constructing reliability-guided self-training targets from self-generated trajectories, without relying on an external verifier or externally annotated corrected trajectories during target construction.
authors: Peng Zhang, Qian Chen, Xianyin Zhang, Yimin Tian, Ruite Fei, Dongyi Lv, Lifan Guo, Chi Zhang, Shuai Liu
bullets: Targets a limitation of prior post-training methods that use one-way teacher supervision or ground-truth trajectories.
Decouples self-generated interleaved rollouts into text and image chains, then assesses each chain’s reliability.
Constructs bidirectional training targets based on the reliability states of the two chains, without external verifiers or corrected annotations.
Improves both generation and understanding on SenseNova-U1 and BAGEL; on SenseNova-U1, GenEval rises from 85.8 to 89.2 and MME from 2282.6 to 2311.6.

papers.abstract: People often make decisions by holistically reasoning over heterogeneous forms of personal information. In this paper, we study the relatively underexplored capability of multimodal personalized reasoning in multimodal large language models (MLLMs). To this end, we introduce \texttt{MPRBench}, a novel and comprehensive benchmark specifically designed to evaluate personalized reasoning across a wide range of tasks and real-world challenges. \texttt{MPRBench} consists of 12 sub-tasks and additionally supports interpretable analysis of representative error cases. Through extensive experiments, we find that current personalized MLLMs still struggle with personalized reasoning due to several key challenges, including inaccurate recognition of personalized concepts and sensitivity to irrelevant personal information. We hope that MPRBench will stimulate further research on personalized reasoning in MLLMs. Code and data are available at https://github.com/kkdh15/MPRBench
authors: Dohyun Kim, Junyong Lhim, Kwanyong Park
bullets: Introduces a benchmark covering multimodal personalized reasoning across 12 sub-tasks and real-world challenges.
Supports interpretable analysis of representative model errors.
Experiments show current personalized MLLMs struggle to recognize personalized concepts accurately.
Models are also sensitive to irrelevant personal information.
Code and data are publicly available via the project repository.

papers.abstract: Cross-modal remote sensing image retrieval (RS-CMIR) requires representations that are simultaneously modality-invariant and semantically discriminative, despite the profound physical gap between heterogeneous sensors such as Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) and multispectral imagery. Recent JEPA-based Predictive self-supervised approaches such as X-JEPA formulate cross-modal alignment as a deterministic latent forecasting task, implicitly assuming uniform patch predictability and leaving cross-modal distributional alignment unaddressed. We propose CAPE-JEPA, a probabilistic cross-modal Joint Embedding Predictive Architecture with three contributions: (i) a cross-attentional Gaussian predictor outputting per-patch parameters (mu, sigma^2) conditioned on opposite-modality context, trained via negative log-likelihood to model inherent cross-sensor prediction uncertainty; (ii) adversarial distributional regularization combining unimodal isotropic Gaussian regularization with a novel cross-modal adversarial variant that aligns modality distributions via worst-case Epps-Pulley characteristic function tests without explicit sample pairing; and (iii) in-training contrastive learning with attention-pooled heads for scene-level discriminative grounding. Evaluated on BigEarthNet-14K (BEN-14K) and fMoW across SAR, multispectral, and RGB modalities, CAPE-JEPA surpasses X-JEPA by up to 13.74 points on BEN-14K and 15.59 points on fMoW, outperforming all baselines including SkySense and CROMA across both unimodal and cross-modal directions while using fewer parameters (407.30M vs. 432.72M).
bullets: Targets the modality gap between SAR, multispectral, and RGB imagery while preserving semantic discrimination.
Uses a cross-attentional Gaussian predictor that estimates per-patch mean and variance and is trained with negative log-likelihood.
Applies unimodal and cross-modal adversarial distribution regularization using Epps–Pulley characteristic-function tests without requiring paired samples.
Adds attention-pooled contrastive learning for scene-level grounding.
Evaluated on BEN-14K and fMoW, it reports gains of up to 13.74 points over X-JEPA on BEN-14K and 15.59 points on fMoW, with fewer parameters.

papers.abstract: Object detection research remains constrained by high annotation costs and the closed-set assumptions of supervised models, limiting scalability to novel categories. We present a target-dataset annotation-free object detection framework that eliminates the need for human labeling on the target dataset by leveraging the complementary strengths of pretrained foundation models, including segmentation and vision-language systems, combined with a self-refining training loop. To further reduce reliance on expensive LVLM queries, we introduce a landmark-based clustering mechanism that amortizes labeling across image clusters, improving label consistency while lowering computational cost. Our method autonomously generates segmentation proposals, assigns semantic labels through multimodal reasoning, and iteratively improves both localization and classification using a lightweight open-set detector. This modular pipeline enables adaptation to completely unseen object classes and domains without any human-provided target-dataset annotations, while maintaining compatibility with existing detection architectures. Evaluations on COCO, LVIS, ODinW-35, and Roboflow-100 demonstrate substantial performance gains over state-of-the-art open-vocabulary and long-tail detection methods, achieving 60.8 AP on COCO and 47.4 AP on LVIS under zero-shot settings. Beyond strong benchmark results, our approach provides a scalable foundation for real-world detection systems in unknown environments, where annotation is infeasible.
bullets: Addresses costly human annotation and the closed-set limitations of supervised detectors.
Generates segmentation proposals, assigns semantic labels through multimodal reasoning, and refines localization and classification iteratively.
Uses landmark-based clustering to amortize LVLM queries, improving label consistency while reducing computational cost.
Supports adaptation to unseen object classes and domains with compatibility across existing detection architectures.
Reports 60.8 AP on COCO and 47.4 AP on LVIS in zero-shot settings, with evaluations across four benchmarks.

This demonstrates that our method not only captures the underlying distribution but also scales to novel concepts beyond the original dataset.

papers.abstract: Multimodal large reasoning models (MLRMs) integrate visual inputs with textual and parametric knowledge, allowing sensitive information to be accessed through cross-modal associations during reasoning. This raises privacy concerns when a visual input should no longer provide access to such information. Machine unlearning can remove this influence without retraining the model from scratch. However, multimodal unlearning methods mainly target samples, concepts, or knowledge content, without separating the knowledge from the cross-modal association through which it is accessed. In reasoning models, target information may disappear from the final answer while remaining in intermediate reasoning, or be replaced by incorrect substitute knowledge. We therefore study cross-modal association unlearning, where the forget target is a designated visual-to-knowledge association: the model should suppress target-bearing behavior under the designated visual context while preserving access to the same knowledge in permitted contexts. We propose Visual-Keyed Counterfactual Rebinding (VKCR), a parameter-efficient framework for cross-modal association editing. VKCR first localizes the edit to a compact association-conditioned parameter subspace. It then reduces support for the designated target at task outputs and counterfactually rebinds the affected reasoning behavior by discouraging target-bearing or unsupported continuations while favoring valid non-sensitive alternatives. We further introduce CLEAR-R and MLLMU-R to evaluate target leakage, hallucinated reassociation, reasoning preservation, and modality-specific utility. Experiments show that VKCR substantially reduces image-conditioned target leakage and hallucinated reassociation, including across heterogeneous task formulations, while preserving non-sensitive visual reasoning and permitted text-only knowledge.
authors: Xinghao Li, Chenchen Tan, Youyang Qu, Shujie Cui, Xingliang Yuan, Cunjian Chen, Chi Liu, Longxiang Gao
bullets: Targets cross-modal associations rather than removing entire samples, concepts, or knowledge.
Localizes edits to a compact association-conditioned parameter subspace for parameter-efficient unlearning.
Uses counterfactual rebinding to suppress target-bearing or unsupported reasoning and favor valid alternatives.
Introduces CLEAR-R and MLLMU-R to assess leakage, hallucinated reassociation, reasoning preservation, and modality-specific utility.
Experiments show reduced image-conditioned leakage and hallucinated reassociation while preserving visual reasoning and text-only access to permitted knowledge.

papers.abstract: Video-LLMs are typically trained on paired video-text data for temporal tasks, yet collecting precise temporal annotations and training on large-scale video datasets are both costly. We investigate whether a text-only LLM, with no vision-language pretraining, can be trained on textual video descriptions alone to perform temporal grounding and receive video only at inference time. This setting removes paired video data from training altogether and is a step toward training multimodal models without paired annotations. We generate a 134K-example corpus of textual sequences with up to 100 time steps, adapt Qwen3-8B with LoRA on CLIP or LLM2CLIP text embeddings, and evaluate on Charades-STA and QV-Highlights without training on videos from either benchmark. LLM2CLIP, whose text encoder supports longer inputs, represents detailed descriptions better than CLIP (61.54 versus 53.86 mtIoU on Temporal-TextVid) and transfers them better to video. Still, replacing text with frame embeddings at inference yields only 4.99 mtIoU on Charades-STA and 11.12 on QV-Highlights, revealing a large modality gap. To bridge it, we propose Nearest Entity Replacement (NER), a training-free mapping that represents each video frame by the normalized mean of its nearest text-entity embeddings, so that the model receives the kind of input it was trained on. NER reaches 14.45 mtIoU on Charades-STA and 20.72 on QV-Highlights, outperforming the strongest of four families of modality-gap baselines by 5.00 and 1.71 points. NER thus enables partial transfer from text to video, while more reliable grounding will likely require encoders with better-aligned text and visual representations.
authors: Divyanshu Mishra, Sabine Sternig, Rakshith Shetty, Erhan Gundogdu
bullets: Motivation: avoid costly paired video-text data and precise temporal annotations by training solely on textual video descriptions.
Method: adapt Qwen3-8B with LoRA on 134K time-indexed text sequences using CLIP or LLM2CLIP text embeddings, then provide video only at inference.
LLM2CLIP transfers better than CLIP, achieving 61.54 vs. 53.86 mtIoU on Temporal-TextVid.
Nearest Entity Replacement maps each frame to nearby text-entity embeddings, improving mtIoU to 14.45 on Charades-STA and 20.72 on QV-Highlights.
Scope: transfer remains partial, indicating that better-aligned text and visual encoders are needed for reliable grounding.

papers.abstract: Segment Anything Model 3 (SAM 3) can segment objects from text prompts and track them across video, but its memory and computation costs make deployment difficult. Post-training quantization (PTQ) reduces these costs by using fewer bits. However, a quantized model can select the wrong object or lose track of its target across frames. We call this prompt-alignment drift. Controlled tests show that perturbing low-variance feature directions strongly affects target selection. We propose Semantics-Preserving Quantization (SPQ), which gives more calibration weight to concept-sensitive parameters, preserves residual features, and corrects the mean error in video memory. Fixed text concepts guide calibration without task annotations. All three components operate offline and add no inference operators. With a W4A8 image encoder, SPQ improves RefCOCO Pr@0.5 from 42.1 to 72.5 over PTQ4SAM while retaining 54.8 COCO mask AP. Experiments on LVIS, RefCOCO variants, and SA-V show consistent gains. A CLIP study also shows improved image-text retrieval.
authors: Xi Xiao, Yunbei Zhang, Lin Zhao, Janet Wang, Xinru Jiang, Yanshu Li, Chenrui Ma, Pan Wang, Tianyang Wang, Xiao Wang
bullets: PTQ can cause prompt-alignment drift, leading to wrong object selection or lost targets across video frames.
SPQ prioritizes concept-sensitive parameters, preserves residual features, and corrects mean error in video memory.
Fixed text concepts guide offline calibration without task annotations; no additional inference operators are required.
With a W4A8 image encoder, SPQ raises RefCOCO Pr@0.5 from 42.1 to 72.5 over PTQ4SAM while retaining 54.8 COCO mask AP.
Consistent gains are reported on LVIS, RefCOCO variants, SA-V, and CLIP image-text retrieval.

papers.abstract: Static and incomplete parametric knowledge limits the performance of multimodal large language models on novel-knowledge and knowledge-intensive tasks, especially those requiring multi-hop evidence acquisition. Existing multimodal agentic search methods often fix visual evidence at the input or a predefined trajectory position, making it difficult for agents to select search modalities as their information needs evolve and to handle complex real-world queries. We define this capability as autonomous cross-modal search: an agent chooses among direct reasoning, text-to-text search, text-to-image search, and reverse-image search, actively introduces visual evidence when appropriate, and switches between and integrates modalities across multiple hops. We propose ModalSearch-Pipeline, a scalable procedure for constructing an interleaved multimodal knowledge graph. It samples paths with diverse depths and modality compositions and uses backward question construction to obscure entity names and image targets that would expose reasoning shortcuts while retaining necessary disambiguating clues, yielding text-only, image-initialized, and arbitrarily interleaved multi-hop problems. We train the ModalSearcher Agent with supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning in a live Web environment, and construct ModalSearch-Bench. Experiments show that ModalSearcher-8B improves average accuracy by 16.2 points over Qwen3-VL-8B under the same agentic workflow across five multimodal knowledge-intensive QA benchmarks, with consistent gains on independently constructed active visual-search benchmarks.
authors: Zhihan Yin, Ruyi Li, Chengyu Fang, Yifeng Yao, Nonghai Zhang, Pengfei Xiong, Terry Zhang, Huishuai Zhang, Dongyan Zhao
bullets: Addresses incomplete parametric knowledge and the rigidity of existing multimodal search trajectories.
Introduces autonomous cross-modal search across direct reasoning, text-to-text, text-to-image, and reverse-image search.
Builds ModalSearch-Pipeline to generate interleaved multimodal knowledge graphs and diverse multi-hop problems.
Trains ModalSearcher with supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning in a live Web environment, alongside ModalSearch-Bench.
ModalSearcher-8B improves average accuracy by 16.2 points over Qwen3-VL-8B across five multimodal QA benchmarks, with consistent gains on active visual-search benchmarks.

papers.abstract: Omni models answer questions about videos by jointly processing sampled frames and audio in one turn, with progress driven largely by scaling model size and omni training data. We ask whether a model needs to hear the audio directly at all, and present SleuthVLM, an agent harness built on a VLM that never hears the audio directly: speech will be transcribed into text, and the VLM will sleuth the video on its own without any predefined workflow. On four omni benchmarks with videos up to 90 minutes, SleuthVLM achieves the best average accuracy: \textbf{75.0%}, 2.6 points above Gemini 3.8 Flash, and it also tops the Video-MME-v2 leaderboard with \textbf{77.8%}; with an open-source 27B VLM, it beats all open-source omni models. We draw three findings: SleuthVLM beats a model that glances; hearing is not the bottleneck, agentic ability is; omni understanding needs better agentic ability, not just more omni data for modality alignment. So we provide a simple but effective starting point for doing omni video understanding. Omni understanding needs better agents, not just bigger models that hear.
authors: Peiran Wu, Fangfei Gou, Zhaoxi Mu, Changhao Zhang, Jian Liu, Weiqiang Wang, Yuntao Wang, Yuanchun Shi, Junxiao Shen
bullets: Challenges the assumption that omni video models must directly hear audio.
Uses a VLM agent that receives speech as text and autonomously investigates video without a predefined workflow.
Achieves 75.0% average accuracy across four omni benchmarks and 77.8% on Video-MME-v2, as reported in the abstract.
With an open-source 27B VLM, outperforms all open-source omni models evaluated.
Concludes that improving agentic reasoning may be more valuable than simply scaling omni data or model size.

papers.title: SleuthVLM: Do We Really Need Audio-in-Video for Omni Video Understanding?
papers.tldr: SleuthVLM shows that strong agentic video reasoning with transcribed speech can outperform models that directly process audio, suggesting agentic ability matters more than audio access.

papers.abstract: Large vision-language models (LVLMs) have recently been extended to handle multiple input images, but this extension dramatically increases the visual token budget, making visual-token pruning not merely an efficiency option but a practical necessity. Existing visual-token pruning methods, primarily designed for the single-image setting, rely on attention-derived saliency signals to estimate per-token importance. However, this attention-centric design transfers poorly to the multi-image regime: it causes substantial performance degradation on multi-image benchmarks, suffers from strong positional bias, and loses discriminative attention signals as the number of input images increases. To test whether attention-selected tokens are truly important for multi-image reasoning, we conduct two complementary causal probes Leave-One-In and Leave-One-Deletion, which measure token importance by restoring individual tokens to a zeroed visual sequence or removing them from the full sequence. Attention-based pruners provide only marginal gains over random selection, showing that attention is a weak proxy for visual-token importance in multi-image reasoning. Motivated by this gap, we propose Relation and Information Aware Pruning (RI-Prune), a training-free, attention-free pre-decoder selector for multi-image visual token pruning. RI-Prune scores each visual token using a z-normalized combination of three signals computed from projector outputs: query relevance, cross-image correspondence with compact per-image prototypes, and intra image representativeness. By integrating these signals, RI-Prune performs balanced per-image Top-K selection to preserve information across input images. Across multiple multi-image benchmarks and three LVLM backbones, RI-Prune achieves a stronger trade-off between token reduction and task performance than prior pruning methods, particularly under aggressive token budgets.
authors: Dongjin Lee, Eunju Lee, Jinhee Jang, Yoonji Lee, Youngbin Kim
bullets: Multi-image inputs greatly increase visual-token budgets, making pruning necessary for practical LVLM inference.
Attention-based pruning transfers poorly to multi-image reasoning due to positional bias and weakening attention signals as image count grows.
Causal Leave-One-In and Leave-One-Deletion probes show attention-selected tokens are only marginally better than random selections.
RI-Prune is a training-free, attention-free pre-decoder selector using three z-normalized projector-output signals.
Balanced per-image Top-K selection preserves information across images and yields a better token-reduction/task-performance trade-off, especially at aggressive budgets.

papers.title: RI-Prune: Relation and Information Aware Visual Token Pruning for Multi-Image Vision-Language Models
papers.tldr: RI-Prune improves multi-image LVLM efficiency by selecting visual tokens using relevance, cross-image relations, and within-image representativeness instead of attention alone.

papers.abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) enables multimodal large language models (MLLMs) to scale capacity efficiently, but expert parameters dominate memory even though only a few experts are activated per token: they account for over 90% of model size in modern MoE-MLLMs (e.g., 54 GB out of about 58 GB in BF16 for InternVL3.5-30B-A3B and Qwen3-VL-30B-A3B). Expert pruning has emerged as an effective compression strategy, but existing methods aggregate importance uniformly across tokens, ignoring that the same expert may serve different roles for vision versus language processing. To address this, we propose MAEP (Modality-Aware Expert Pruning), a training-free framework that decomposes expert importance by modality in a single forward pass. MAEP introduces (1) Delta-H Output ($\Delta H$), a redistribution-aware metric measuring the MoE output change when an expert is removed, and (2) low-attention vision tokens as a vision-side pruning signal that is dataset-stable: its expert-importance ranking remains stable across different datasets. Text-side importance serves as a preservation signal while vision-side importance serves as a pruning signal, and experts are ranked globally across layers. Experiments on three MoE-based MLLMs across multimodal and text benchmarks show that MAEP outperforms modality-agnostic baselines on the majority of multimodal benchmarks while remaining competitive on text-only tasks, reducing the BF16 expert weight footprint by about 27 GB (about 47% of total memory) so that the full weight footprint of an approximately 58 GB model fits within a single 40 GB GPU. Code is available at https://github.com/nota-github/MAEP.
bullets: Targets MoE expert parameters, which dominate the memory footprint of multimodal large language models.
Separates expert importance for vision and language in a single forward pass using redistribution-aware output change and low-attention vision tokens.
Uses text-side importance for preservation, vision-side importance for pruning, and globally ranks experts across layers.
Across three MoE-MLLMs, outperforms modality-agnostic pruning on most multimodal benchmarks and remains competitive on text-only tasks.
Reduces the BF16 expert footprint by about 27 GB, enabling an approximately 58 GB model to fit on one 40 GB GPU.

papers.abstract: Recycling a target model's own predictions offers a training-free source of proposals for speculative decoding. In vision-language models, however, existing recycling indexes predictions by the last token alone, conflating predictions computed under different images and prefixes; we find that such reuse fails most often at image-sensitive decoding states. Longer keys reduce this aliasing but match fewer states. We introduce \method, which stores target predictions under one-, two-, and three-token keys: contextual memories live only for the current request and are thus implicitly conditioned on its image, while token-level memory persists across requests to retain coverage. At each lookup, entropy-confidence weighting fuses the retrieved predictions according to their key specificity and concentration. Best-first search composes the fused transitions into a candidate tree, supplemented by suffix-matched continuations, and one target pass verifies the tree under greedy decoding. Without training or an auxiliary draft model, \method\ achieves mean speedups over autoregressive decoding of $1.66\speed$ and $1.56\speed$ across seven single-turn benchmarks on Qwen2.5-VL-7B and LLaVA-1.6-7B, exceeding the strongest training-free baseline, Token Recycling ($1.51\speed$ and $1.37\speed$). Our implementation is available in https://github.com/Senmo996/RECAP-official-code.
authors: Hengjie Zhu, Dayan Wu, Xinze Liu, Peng Fu, Zheng Lin, Weiping Wang
bullets: Addresses prediction reuse errors caused by indexing only the last token, especially at image-sensitive states.
Combines request-local one-, two-, and three-token memories with persistent token-level memory to balance specificity and coverage.
Uses entropy-confidence weighting, best-first candidate-tree construction, suffix continuations, and one target pass for greedy verification.
Reports mean speedups of 1.66× on Qwen2.5-VL-7B and 1.56× on LLaVA-1.6-7B across seven single-turn benchmarks.
Outperforms the cited Token Recycling baseline, which achieves 1.51× and 1.37× respectively; results are scoped to the evaluated models and benchmarks.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) have demonstrated significant advances in reasoning with visual data, which is particularly important given that much of human knowledge is encoded visually in scientific articles and other sources. However, a gap remains in understanding how artificial agents, powered by VLMs, perceive and navigate decision-making under uncertainty in the presence of visual data. This study explores this gap by evaluating and analyzing autonomous decision-making processes. Building upon prior work in visualization literacy and decision theory, we conducted two complementary studies: one examining how agents perceive and quantify uncertainty encoded in visualizations, and another investigating how artificial agents make decisions based on visual data in the form of images. We analyzed perception accuracy and decision performance across models and visualization types. Our results show that GPT-4o demonstrates the highest accuracy in perceiving uncertainty in pie and bar charts among the tested models. For decision-making, autonomous agents showed the best alignment with rational decision theory when uncertainty was represented through circle charts, icon arrays, or text.
bullets: Investigates artificial agents’ decision-making under uncertainty using visual information.
Conducts two studies: uncertainty perception in visualizations and decisions based on images.
Analyzes perception accuracy and decision performance across models and visualization formats.
GPT-4o achieved the highest uncertainty-perception accuracy for tested pie and bar charts.
Agents aligned most closely with rational decision theory when uncertainty was shown through circle charts, icon arrays, or text.

papers.abstract: Connecting a DNA foundation model to a large language model (LLM) usually requires training a connector, and often the LLM too. We show that a closed-form map is enough for gene-level questions. Our method, the socket, fits one ridge regression (the plug) from frozen Evo 2 features to the host LLM's own representation of the gene's symbol, name, and description at an early layer. The plug's output replaces the hidden state at placeholder positions, and no gradient passes through the host. We test it on GeneHop, a five-way multiple-choice benchmark split by homology. In a single run on the held-out test set, under a frozen analysis plan, real DNA beats shuffled DNA on all four hosts: by +22.2 points [19.8, 25.0] on Qwen3.5-4B, +26.1 [24.3, 27.9] on Qwen3.6-27B, +16.7 [14.2, 19.7] on Mistral-7B, and +18.4 [16.2, 21.0] on OLMo-2-7B. All four survive Holm correction, every null control stays within two points of the sham level, and the development results agree within 2.3 points. A layer rule that uses no task items was selected on three hosts; it predicted the working layer of the fourth before any DNA-plug scoring on it. A text-only linear map lets one plug feed any other host, at a cost of at most 0.9 points on test. The socket conveys gene identity: nearest-neighbour retrieval recovers 72-84% of the effect, but the plug beats it on every host by 3.0-5.2 points and keeps most of its effect without training homologs.
bullets: Maps frozen Evo 2 gene features to early-layer LLM representations of gene symbols, names, and descriptions.
Uses one closed-form ridge fit; the host LLM receives the mapped output at placeholder positions without gradient-based training.
On GeneHop, real DNA improved five-way accuracy over shuffled DNA by 16.7–26.1 points across four LLMs, with all effects surviving correction.
Null controls stayed near sham levels, development results matched test results closely, and a task-independent layer rule generalized across hosts.
The socket primarily conveys gene identity, but outperformed nearest-neighbour retrieval by 3.0–5.2 points and transferred across hosts with at most a 0.9-point test cost.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) increasingly support construction hazard monitoring, yet their frequent false alarms remain poorly understood. This study investigates whether false struck-by hazard warnings arise from failures in object recognition, spatial relation encoding, or hazard decisions dominated by learned co-occurrence priors. We evaluated Qwen2.5-VL-7B and InternVL3.5-8B using 355 counterfactual worker-excavator scene pairs with controlled spatial proximity and worker-removal variants, combining behavioral analysis, internal representation probing, causal interventions, and decision correction. Both models recognized the entities and encoded their spatial relations (out-of-fold AUROC: 0.82 and 0.91), assigning higher hazard scores to near than far scenes in 79% and 73% of pairs. Nevertheless, 74% and 100% of far scenes were falsely classified as hazardous. Removing the worker reduced Qwen's hazard rate to 11%, while worker presence exerted 2.4- and 3.2-times greater influence on hazard scores than spatial proximity in the respective models. Attention-head interventions, neuron-level interventions, and activation steering failed to eliminate this co-occurrence bias. However, conditioning hazard decisions on the model's own spatial-relation representation improved Qwen's specificity from 0.36 to 0.58 at matched sensitivity, outperforming threshold recalibration. These findings reveal that VLM struck-by false alarms stem primarily from decision-making failures rather than deficiencies in object recognition or spatial encoding, suggesting that future efforts should prioritize conditioning hazard decisions on encoded spatial evidence rather than further improving visual recognition alone.
bullets: Evaluated Qwen2.5-VL-7B and InternVL3.5-8B on 355 counterfactual worker–excavator scene pairs.

Conditioning decisions on encoded spatial relations improved Qwen’s specificity from 0.36 to 0.58 at matched sensitivity.

papers.selection_reason: Analyzes spatial-relation encoding and co-occurrence bias in vision-language models for hazard detection; relevant to spatial intelligence in multimodal foundation models.
papers.title: Co-Occurrence Priors Override Visual Spatial Evidence: Understanding False Alarms in Vision-Language Models for Construction Struck-By Hazard Detection
papers.tldr: VLMs can recognize workers, excavators, and their spatial relations yet still issue false struck-by alarms because hazard decisions are dominated by worker–excavator co-occurrence priors.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) are increasingly used for AI-generated image (AIGI) detection, providing natural-language explanations for authenticity judgments. However, their ability to interpret text within images may also expose these judgments to misleading semantic cues. We systematically evaluate typographic attack strategies across detection-oriented, open-weight, and commercial VLMs, considering both real-to-fake and fake-to-real attacks. Our results show that reasoning modes generally exhibit greater vulnerability than direct modes and that attack effectiveness exhibits pronounced directional asymmetry. Moreover, larger models tend to exhibit higher clean detection accuracy but also higher attack success rates. We further examine attack robustness under image and text transformations and investigate whether overlays indicating the correct class can aid error correction. Together, these analyses characterize how typographic attacks influence authenticity judgments and expose limitations of current VLM-based AIGI detection systems.
bullets: Evaluates typographic attacks against detection-oriented, open-weight, and commercial VLMs.

papers.abstract: Effective human-AI collaboration requires partners to establish references through interaction, which becomes fragile when descriptions are ambiguous, similar referents compete, or partners see different things. We study referential uncertainty - uncertainty over which candidate object a description refers to - in a collaborative puzzle task where a human Helper instructs an AI Worker to place pieces. The Worker must identify and communicate its uncertainty, and the Helper must recognize and act on it. We show that a separately elicited belief distribution over candidate pieces is better calibrated (ECE 0.15) and better discriminates correct from incorrect placements (AUROC 0.65) than raw action-token probabilities, which are severely overconfident (0.97 mean confidence, ECE 0.44). Across three frontier vision-language models (GPT-4.1, GPT-5, GPT-5.5), this elicited uncertainty rises predictably with instruction vagueness, but not with competing referents in context, even when those increase errors. The models seldom externalize it, asking for clarification on only 3.5-16.7% of turns. In a controlled human study (N=210), participants given only the Worker's default message accept 78% of wrong placements and cannot tell right from wrong (AUC 0.50). Precise descriptions and, especially, well-targeted hedges cut wrong-move acceptance to 36% while largely preserving correct-move acceptance, compensating for missing shared awareness such as not seeing the Worker's action. But this benefit depends on targeting: a deployable hedge derived from the model's own belief entropy inherits that signal's weakness and can do more harm than good. Externalized uncertainty helps a human partner only when it is accurately targeted.
bullets: Studies referential uncertainty in a collaborative puzzle task where an AI places pieces based on human instructions.
Elicited belief distributions over candidate pieces are better calibrated and discriminative than raw action-token probabilities, which are overconfident.
Across GPT-4.1, GPT-5, and GPT-5.5, uncertainty increases with vague instructions but often misses competing referents that cause errors.
Models ask for clarification infrequently, and humans given default messages accept many incorrect placements without distinguishing them from correct ones.
Precise descriptions and targeted hedges reduce wrong-move acceptance, but entropy-based hedges can be counterproductive when uncertainty is misaligned.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. The collaborative puzzle task and the human study conditions. The partners hold asymmetric information: the Worker (AI) sees the current board and all 24 available pieces but not the target, whereas theHelper (human) sees the target pattern but neither the pieces nor—by default—the Worker’s board. The Helper gives a referring instruction and the Worker selects, places a piece, and replies with a message (here, a blue spiral placed in the target slot). Each condition changes exactly one element of this same turn. Four vary only the Worker’s message while the board stays hidden: Generic (A) is the original message; Described (C) appends a precise description of the placed piece; and Hedged (D) and Self-hedged (E) additionally append an expression of uncertainty—inserted by an oracle on the objectively wrong turns (D) or, in the deployable variant, from the Worker’s own belief entropy (E). The fifth condition, Visible board, keeps the Generic message but reveals the Worker’s board to the Helper—the shared-view control (A/shared). Holding the turn fixed and varying only the message or the board’s visibility isolates how each externalized signal shapes the Helper’s perceived confidence, error detection, and willingness to act.
Fig. 5. Clarification rates on turns with incorrect piece selected (could benefit from clarification) and correct select piece (would not benefit from clarification) across models model.

Fig. 6. Elicited uncertainty as an externalization signal (image modality). (Left) the no-action (question) rate rises with the model’s own elicited belief entropy for all three models—they question more when their belief is more spread out. (Right) ROC of the rule “hedge if belief entropy ≥ 𝜏” for predicting the model’s own wrong placements (scored vs. ground truth piece); all three curves sit close to the diagonal (AUROC 0.55–0.66), so belief entropy is only a weak error predictor. Models externalize uncertainty in proportion to a signal that is itself too weak to cleanly trigger a hedge.

Fig. 3. Instruction specificity (image modality) results per model. (left) stacked outcome composition of Worker response (correct piece / wrong piece / no-action) at each specificity level from overspecified (L1) to vague (L4), with the original utterance (L0) placed between L2 and L3 as the baseline (dashed); the right panel shows mean belief entropy. Accuracy falls and belief entropy rises with vagueness for all models.

Fig. 4. Board confusability (image modality) results per model. (left) stacked outcome composition of Worker responses (correct piece / wrong piece / no-action) and (right) mean belief entropy on a distinct board (B1), the original board (B0), and a confusable board (B2), in order of increasing confusability. Accuracy falls sharply while no-action and belief entropy barely move.

Fig. 2. Reliability curves for the uncertainty signals: (Right) Raw action-token probabilities are over-confident; temperature scaling reduces the gap. (Left) The separately elicited belief provides the strongest combined discrimination and calibration. (Bottom) Distribution of confidence on the placed piece, split by whether the placement was correct or wrong.

Fig. 14. The grading interface (one trial, Generic condition). In this between-subjects study, each participant reviews the flattened interaction up to the current turn and judges the AI Worker’s placement. (a) The dialogue—the Worker’s opening status, the Helper’s instruction (here “bold diagonal lines on a white background”), and the Worker’s placement message. For that message the participant reports two 0–100 judgements, (b) apparent confidence (how confident the Worker sounds) and (c) correctness likelihood (how likely the intended piece was placed), and (d) chooses a single action: proceed, ask the Worker to change/undo, ask it to explain/verify, or give a more specific instruction. (e) As the Helper, the participant sees the target pattern but not the Worker’s board; the board is revealed only in the Visible-board condition. Across conditions we vary only the Worker’s message and board visibility (Table 1), holding the task turns fixed. The available pieces are not shown in any condition as they are also not available to see for the Helper.

Fig. 13. Board confusability (text modality) results per model. (left) stacked outcome composition of Worker responses (correct piece / wrong piece / no-action) and (right) mean belief entropy on a distinct board (B1), the original board (B0), and a confusable board (B2), in order of increasing confusability. Accuracy falls sharply while no-action and belief entropy barely move.

Fig. 11. Instruction specificity (text modality) results per model. (left) stacked outcome composition of Worker response (correct piece / wrong piece / no-action) at each specificity level from overspecified (L1) to vague (L4), with the original utterance (L0) placed between L2 and L3 as the baseline (dashed); the right panel shows mean belief entropy. Accuracy falls and belief entropy rises with vagueness for all models.

Fig. 12. Board (environmental) confusability. The same fixed referring instruction (“place the spiral piece”) is shown against three boards along a confusability axis; the instruction is held constant so that only the competing referents change. Distinct (B1): the target is the only piece of its shape family and thus the sole plausible referent. Baseline (B0): the real board seen in the dialogue, where a couple of incidental look-alikes occur naturally. Confusable (B2): five same-family, same-thickness look-alikes are inserted, burying the target among near-identical distractors. The red ring marks the intended target; the blue ring marks a confusable same-family look-alike. Moving from distinct to confusable makes it increasingly likely that the Worker commits to a look-alike—the environmental (referent-side) axis of referential uncertainty, complementary to instruction vagueness (Fig. 3).

papers.tldr: Human–AI collaboration improves when AI uncertainty about ambiguous references is accurately identified and communicated, but current models rarely externalize it and poorly targeted hedges can hurt.

papers.abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) improves reasoning by providing token-level supervision from a teacher on a student's own trajectories. Existing methods primarily focus on enhancing this teacher-side guidance (e.g., by enriching teacher inputs and refining teacher feedback), yet we find that limited student perception is another critical bottleneck in multimodal OPD. By providing oracle visual facts, the performance of OPD-trained students can still be substantially improved for both weak and strong teachers. To address this bottleneck, we propose S-OPD, a simple multimodal on-policy distillation framework that explicitly strengthens student perceptual learning through two objectives. Specifically, Teacher-calibrated Policy Contrast separates student policies under original and masked images with teacher-based token-level gating, strengthening the student's reliance on visual evidence during reasoning. Policy Agreement aligns student policies under original and noise-perturbed images, further improving perceptual robustness to visual noise. Notably, our method can be seamlessly plugged into existing OPD frameworks, requiring no additional data annotations, model parameters or inference operations. Extensive experiments on eight benchmarks across student scales and distillation paradigms demonstrate consistent performance improvements, with gains of up to 4.25 points on LogicVista. When combined with existing teacher-side supervision methods, our method can yield further gains. Code is available at https://github.com/Sirilaw/S-OPD.
bullets: Student perception is a key bottleneck in multimodal OPD, beyond improving teacher supervision.
Teacher-calibrated Policy Contrast uses teacher-gated token supervision to distinguish original from masked-image policies.
Policy Agreement aligns predictions across original and noise-perturbed images for greater visual-noise robustness.
The framework plugs into existing OPD methods without extra annotations, parameters, or inference operations.
Experiments across student scales and distillation settings show consistent improvements, reaching up to 4.25 points on LogicVista.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models increasingly pair a pre-trained vision-language model (VLM) with a flow-matching expert that conditions its action predictions on the VLM's key-value representations. Those representations must carry information useful for control, yet the VLM was never trained for the action expert's flow-matching objective. Two signals can address this: gradients backpropagated from the expert's loss (coupling), or VLM supervision to predict discrete tokens encoding the same target actions. Prominent training recipes forgo the first, blocking expert-to-VLM gradients (insulation) to protect the VLM's existing capabilities, while also supervising it on vision-language data and action tokens. Because vision-language co-training also aims to preserve those capabilities, the additional protection provided by insulation is unclear. At the same time, insulation removes a direct signal about which features continuous action prediction requires. On the other hand, action-token supervision offers an alternative way to learn action-relevant representations, which may explain why insulation succeeds in practice. We disentangle these factors in autonomous driving and manipulation by independently varying action-token supervision and whether the expert's loss updates the VLM. In open-loop driving, insulation is competitive with coupling when action tokens are supervised; without them, coupling reduces trajectory-prediction error by roughly 25%. When both components are trained jointly from the outset, coupling increases closed-loop driving route progress by approximately 17% with action-token supervision and 40% without it, and similarly improves robot manipulation performance under both settings. These findings show that the value of gradient insulation depends on the VLM's action supervision and the evaluation setting, challenging insulation as a default VLA training recipe.
authors: Asher James Hancock, Boyi Li, Yuxiao Chen, Shuhan Tan, Wenhao Ding, Thomas Tian, Yan Wang, Boris Ivanovic, Marco Pavone
bullets: VLA training can provide action information through expert-loss gradients, discrete action-token supervision, or both.
The study independently varies gradient routing and action-token supervision in autonomous driving and robot manipulation.
With action-token supervision, insulation is competitive in open-loop driving; without it, coupling lowers trajectory-prediction error by roughly 25%.
When trained jointly from the start, coupling improves closed-loop route progress by approximately 17% with action tokens and 40% without them, while also improving manipulation performance.
The benefit of insulation depends on supervision and evaluation setting rather than being universally protective of VLM capabilities.

papers.title: Should the Action Expert Train the VLM? Action-Token Supervision and Gradient Routing in Mixture-of-Transformer VLAs
papers.tldr: Gradient coupling from the action expert to the VLM can substantially improve VLA control, especially when action-token supervision is absent, challenging gradient insulation as a default.

papers.abstract: Composed Image Retrieval (CIR) aims to retrieve a target image given a reference image and a modification text. Although recent approaches leveraging Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have shown significant progress, we argue that the MLLM's compositional understanding remains underutilized. This stems from directly mapping composed queries into a retrieval embedding via contrastive supervision alone, without explicitly resolving the intended visual modifications. In this work, we introduce Factorized MLLM Embeddings (FactEmbed), which decouples compositional query comprehension from building discriminative embeddings. Rather than directly projecting the composed query into a single embedding without internal reasoning, FactEmbed employs a set of factorized latents that simulate the intended visual modifications via an intermediate target imagination objective. This process encourages the latents to ground into target semantics before forming discriminative representations for retrieval. Subsequently, to propagate these factorized representations throughout the model for retrieval, we optimize a factor-level contrastive loss while distilling the decomposed representations into a deeper attention layer of the MLLM. Finally, for efficient inference, we retain the [EOS] token to establish a global-level embedding on top of these factorized latents, while we exploit the mean-pooled factorized latents to rerank a short candidate list at negligible cost, as both are produced by the same forward pass. Extensive evaluations demonstrate that FactEmbed outperforms prior works across CIR benchmarks.
authors: WonJun Moon, Seongchan Kim, Dahun Kim, Seungryong Kim
bullets: Addresses the underuse of MLLM compositional understanding when queries are trained only with direct contrastive supervision.
Uses factorized latents and an intermediate target-imagination objective to ground intended modifications in target-image semantics.
Applies factor-level contrastive learning and distills decomposed representations into a deeper MLLM attention layer.
Combines an [EOS]-based global embedding with mean-pooled factorized latents for low-cost candidate reranking in one forward pass.
Reports improved performance over prior methods across CIR benchmarks.
