papers.tldr: FactEmbed improves composed image retrieval by explicitly modeling visual modifications with factorized MLLM latents before constructing retrieval embeddings.

papers.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) allow social scientists to analyze video at scale, but researchers must decide which parts of a video to provide as input. We use the term representation validity to examine how text, audio, video, and combined inputs affect measurement and subsequent analysis. We compare input representations across six open-weight MLLMs and three human-annotated video datasets. No representation consistently performs best. On seven news-related constructs, native-video performance varies little across models (macro-F1 = .70-.77), while extracted-text performance ranges from .52 to .80. Three models perform better with text and three with video. Combining inputs rarely improves performance. Higher classification accuracy also does not reliably produce estimates closer to those based on human codes. The highest-F1 representation best reproduces human-coded regression coefficients in 17 of 42 comparisons. Even when each model uses its highest-F1 deployable representation, 45% of sample-prevalence estimates differ from the human-coded benchmark by more than ten percentage points. Input representation therefore requires validation for both the construct being measured and the quantity estimated from the resulting labels.
authors: Christian Pipal, Eva-Maria Vogel, Morgan Wack
bullets: The study examines how text, audio, video, and combined inputs affect measurement validity in MLLM-based video analysis.
Across six open-weight MLLMs and three human-annotated video datasets, no input representation consistently performs best.
Native-video macro-F1 varies little across models (.70–.77), while extracted-text performance varies more widely (.52–.80).
Combining modalities rarely improves classification, and higher accuracy does not reliably yield human-aligned regression or prevalence estimates.
Even with each model’s best deployable representation, 45% of prevalence estimates differed from human-coded benchmarks by more than ten percentage points.

papers.abstract: Vision-language verifiers judge whether an image faithfully matches a textual description, yet existing training pipelines typically rely on static supervision from stronger external judges or curated hard-negative data. Such supervision requires external generation or annotation, is teacher-bounded, and is difficult to adapt as model failures evolve. We introduce PROVE (Perturb-and-Repair Optimization for Vision-Language Evaluation), a self-play framework that trains verifiers through a closed perturb-verify-repair-verify loop. Starting from a known-correct image-caption pair, a Mutator introduces a typed perturbation over objects, attributes, counts, or relations. The verifier then judges the perturbed caption and provides textual feedback, which a Repairer uses to recover a faithful caption for re-verification. These two verification rounds produce structured rewards for informative mismatches and visually grounded repairs. Since perturbation, verification, and repair are role-conditioned behaviors of the same evolving multimodal backbone, updating the shared parameters also improves the verifier itself. Experiments show that PROVE improves fine-grained compositional verification across model scales and families and strengthens visual-detail robustness on the reference backbone, with limited, benchmark-dependent changes on broader multimodal tasks.
authors: Zijun Huang, Yingjun Du, Cees G. M. Snoek
bullets: Targets compositional image-caption verification involving objects, attributes, counts, and relations.
Uses a shared multimodal backbone as Mutator, Verifier, and Repairer in a closed-loop training process.
Derives rewards from detecting informative mismatches and producing visually grounded repairs.
Improves fine-grained compositional verification across model scales and families.
Enhances visual-detail robustness, while broader multimodal-task gains are limited and benchmark-dependent.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of PROVE. A single Qwen backbone is reused under three role prompts: Mutator, Verifier, and Repairer. Given a clean image-caption pair, the Mutator produces a localized caption perturbation, e.g., changing an attribute from “red” to “blue”, to create a hard image-text mismatch. The Verifier first judges the perturbed caption and returns a decision-feedback pair (y1, r1) that diagnoses the mismatch. Conditioned on this feedback, the Repairer generates a revised caption, which is then checked by the same Verifier to obtain (y2, r2). Rewards from the two verification rounds train the shared model with DrGRPO, so perturbation, verification, and repair co-evolve within one multimodal backbone.

Figure 4: Qualitative verifier examples. Each panel compares the base Qwen3.5-2B model with PROVE on a fine-grained verification case. The examples cover relation, object existence, attribute, and counting errors. PROVE better localizes the relevant visual evidence and avoids accepting captions or answers that miss the targeted mismatch.

Figure 3: Self-play dynamics and axis-level gains. (a) The Repairer steadily improves in repair success and structural alignment, while the verifier pass rate rises as repairs catch up with the current Mutator distribution; the dashed line marks the lower finite-group maximum-variance reference at 1/3 (Appendix F). (b) Each panel compares Qwen3.5-2B with PROVE on an aggregated visual-semantic capability; Total is the overall average in Table 1. The largest gains appear on attribute and relation verification, matching the typed perturbation axes used during self-play.

(b) Existing verifier training relies on static external supervision, while (c) PROVE creates adaptive supervision through a perturb–verify–repair– verify self-play loop.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces a self-play verification framework for vision-language composition understanding with a shared multimodal backbone.
papers.title: Perturb, Repair, Verify: Self-Play Vision-Language Verifiers for Compositional Understanding
papers.tldr: PROVE trains vision-language verifiers through self-play perturbation, feedback, repair, and re-verification instead of relying on external judges or curated hard negatives.

papers.abstract: Multimodal discrete diffusion language models (dLLMs) generate responses through iterative mask prediction and offer a promising alternative to autoregressive large vision-language models. However, they still suffer from hallucination, producing outputs that are plausible under language priors but insufficiently grounded in the image. We argue that hallucination in multimodal dLLMs is not only a token prediction problem, but also a premature commitment problem: during iterative denoising, some masked positions are unmasked too early because their confidence is driven more by language priors than by visual evidence, and these early commitments can bias later generation. To address this issue, we propose Visual Gain Ordering (VIGOR), a training-free and plug-and-play inference strategy that reorders masked positions according to counterfactual visual evidence. At each denoising step, VIGOR compares the confidence of each candidate token under the original image-conditioned pass and an additional visual-ablation pass, and prioritizes positions whose predictions are more strongly supported by the image. Experiments on LLaDA-V and Lumina-DiMOO show that VIGOR consistently reduces hallucination and improves multimodal reasoning performance across benchmarks. Code is available at https://github.com/THU-BPM/Vigor.
authors: Junzhe Chen, Tian Qin, Eugenie Shi, Tianshu Zhang, Qiang Ju, Lijie Wen
bullets: Targets premature token commitments during iterative denoising, which can amplify image-ungrounded predictions.
Uses a training-free, plug-and-play inference strategy requiring no model retraining.
Compares token confidence with and without visual input to estimate counterfactual visual support.
Prioritizes masked positions whose predictions gain more from the image.
Experiments on LLaDA-V and Lumina-DiMOO report consistent hallucination reduction and improved multimodal reasoning across benchmarks.

papers.title: VIGOR: Visual Gain Ordering for Hallucination Mitigation in Multimodal Discrete Diffusion Language Models

papers.abstract: Complex visual question answering often requires vision-language models to think with images, i.e., actively acquire local visual evidence by zooming into informative regions of high-resolution images. Our error analysis shows that many failures in this setting originate from incorrect observation actions, where the model fails to localize key regions or obtain crops that contain sufficient evidence for answering. We further observe that bounding-box tokens exhibit substantially higher generation entropy than ordinary language tokens, indicating high uncertainty when the model decides where to look. However, existing reinforcement learning methods based on final-answer rewards provide only trajectory-level feedback, making it difficult to assign precise credit to the observation actions. We propose Observation Policy Optimization (OPO), an RL algorithm for optimizing observation actions in tool-augmented thinking with images. OPO consists of two core modules. First, Uncertainty-Guided Observation Branching (UOB) treats each image zoom-in tool call as an observation event and selectively branches at high-uncertainty, low-redundancy events during rollout, enabling efficient exploration of alternative cropping decisions and their resulting visual evidence. Second, Evidence-Localized Advantage Attribution (ELAA) compares sibling branches using local evidence-sufficiency rewards and assigns credit only to the corresponding observation-action tokens. By decoupling observation-action optimization from trajectory-level outcome supervision, OPO improves visual evidence acquisition and further enhances visual reasoning performance. Experiments show that OPO consistently improves Qwen3-VL models across scales and achieves competitive performance against larger models and tool-augmented baselines. Code is publicly available.
authors: Junfeng Wang, Jiawei Liu, Yongchao Xu, Tao Jiang, Jiangbo Ai, Jin Zhang, Chong Wang, Qixing Zhang
bullets: Visual question-answering failures often stem from poor zoom or cropping decisions rather than language reasoning.
Bounding-box decisions have high uncertainty, while final-answer rewards provide weak, trajectory-level credit for these actions.
OPO uses Uncertainty-Guided Observation Branching to explore alternative crops at uncertain, nonredundant observation events.
Evidence-Localized Advantage Attribution assigns local evidence-based credit to the observation actions responsible for each branch’s outcome.
Experiments show consistent improvements across Qwen3-VL model scales, with competitive performance versus larger and tool-augmented models.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of OPO. UOB concentrates rollout exploration around high-uncertainty and low-redundancy observation decisions by branching from the shared pre-tool prefix. ELAA then compares sibling crops within each branch group using evidence-sufficiency rewards and assigns the resulting local advantage only to the observation-action tokens.

papers.selection_reason: RL-based optimization of observation and zoom actions for vision-language models, directly relevant to multimodal foundation models and spatial evidence acquisition.
papers.title: Learning Where to Look: Observation Policy Optimization for Thinking with Images
papers.tldr: Observation Policy Optimization improves image-based reasoning by training models to choose more informative regions to inspect.

papers.abstract: Video generation has progressed from isolated clips to coherent short-form audiovisual sequences, and the bottleneck is shifting from rendering to semantic control. This report summarizes the observations and insights on multimodal understanding gained from successive generations of Kling. We argue that generation quality is the projection of multimodal understanding through the entire data--conditioning--alignment--evaluation chain, and we examine this chain module by module. Kling-MLLM, a shared multimodal foundation model that unifies image, video, audio, synchronized audio--video, and interleaved inputs, is specialized for each downstream module. Because a DiT is trained on far fewer training samples than a language model, we treat captioning as a semantic contract that maximizes description density, and extend it to reference-grounded captioning that makes reference bindings explicit. Prompt enhancement translates user intent into this caption distribution: basic PE is derived from captions of compelling videos and refined with text-level and generator-in-the-loop reinforcement learning, while agentic PE refines the story and retrieves compelling examples. We show that a reliable text encoder comes from perceptual training rather than from stronger language ability, and that candidates can be screened from text alone before end-to-end training. Reward modeling pairs a general reward model for explainable, localized critiques with a decision reward model for fast multidimensional scoring, treating perceptual bandwidth as a first-class design parameter. Finally, we review task-specific automatic evaluation, focusing on protocols that expose scoring shortcuts and help trace failures to their upstream source. We hope these lessons offer practical guidance for building the understanding stack behind controllable video generation.

papers.abstract: Large vision-language models (LVLMs) can process interleaved text and multiple images in a single context, but how they internally identify the image relevant to a question remains poorly understood. We study this grounding step as in-context image retrieval and introduce ICIR-MCQ, a controlled probe for head-level analysis of image retrieval. Using each head's attention mass over image-token spans, we first identify sparse pointer heads that reliably point to the target image. These heads transfer beyond the probe: a single pointer head is competitive with external vision-language retrievers on a naturalistic multi-image retrieval benchmark, showing that LVLMs contain a strong internal image retrieval signal. Attention alone, however, shows where a head reads from, not what its output passes on to later layers, so we introduce a complementary output-side analysis. For each head, we train a lightweight image retriever on its value-weighted output and use it to identify writer heads, whose outputs contain enough information to identify the target image. Surprisingly, the pointer and writer criteria select substantially different head sets, with only 35 to 47 heads overlapping among the top-100 heads under each criterion. Targeted set-partition ablations show that the heads most important for standard multi-image inference are concentrated in this pointer-writer intersection, while heads selected by only one criterion show less consistent separation from random-head controls. The most consistent causal effects arise from heads selected by both the attention-based pointer and output-side writer criteria. Code and data: https://github.com/parkquasar/Image-Retrieval-Heads.

papers.abstract: Multimodal agents use web and image tools to answer questions beyond their internal knowledge. Some search tasks use images mainly to identify an initial entity, then rely on text retrieval. These tasks offer limited insight into how agents connect information across images, objects, and search steps. We therefore focus on visual context management. This involves organizing and using visual information and linking it to other findings during search. Visually intensive tasks require agents to combine object appearance, local details, or spatial relations with external information. We introduce VisSearch-Bench, with 204 human-written tasks across 7 main domains and 25 subdomains. It covers Set-wise Visual Search, Sequential Visual Search, Hybrid Wide-Deep Search, Competitive Visual Disambiguation, and Visual-Structure-Guided Search. Each task provides a reference answer, traceable evidence, and scoring rules. Accuracy measures complete task success, while Process Score measures the correctness and completeness of individual results and subquestion answers. Across 16 multimodal models, the best system fully solves only 26.47% of tasks, even with search tools. These results highlight the challenge of linking visual evidence with search results to produce complete answers.

papers.abstract: Optical Character Recognition (OCR) is among the oldest and most widely deployed applications of artificial intelligence. This survey reviews its development, focusing on the Foundation Model Era. We define OCR through faithful transcription: within a specified visual scope, OCR should completely reconstruct the text, notation, and document structure observable in the source image, and every textual, notational, or structural element in the output must be verifiable from visual evidence in that image. We trace the development from specialist OCR models toward unified models, examining joint text detection and recognition, structured sequence generation, and the use of pretrained vision-language models (VLMs). We organize contemporary OCR systems into five coexisting families: modular toolkits and task-specific models, specialized document VLMs, hybrid workflows, general-purpose VLMs, and commercial products and managed services. We compare their architectures, data, and training, examining hallucination and omission, insufficient spatial grounding, and inference cost in generative OCR. We review evaluation from character and scene text recognition to parsing individual structural elements and full-page transcription, highlighting gaps in consistent output definitions, attribution of performance to individual components, and coverage of real capture conditions and visible content and structure. Finally, we summarize the challenges facing OCR and discuss directions for future research. We continuously track related work at https://github.com/zhihengli-casia/Awesome-OCR-in-the-Foundation-Model-Era.

Reviews joint detection-recognition, structured generation, and pretrained vision-language model approaches.
Highlights generative OCR challenges including hallucinations, omissions, weak spatial grounding, and inference cost.
Identifies evaluation gaps involving output definitions, component attribution, real-world capture conditions, and visible structural content.

papers.abstract: Nighttime images are inherently susceptible to complex, compound degradations, making accurate quality assessment exceptionally challenging. Score-based IQA methods condense quality into a single number, lacking the multi-dimensional, language-grounded reasoning required for nighttime evaluation. Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) offer a more comprehensive alternative, yet remain constrained by a critical data gap: existing real-world IQA datasets are overwhelmingly daytime-centric and often built from outdated captures, while synthetic alternatives lack nighttime-specific degradation modeling, yielding artifacts far removed from authentic nighttime conditions. To bridge this gap, we present NightIQA, a dataset and benchmark suite purpose-built for MLLM-based nighttime IQA. It comprises three core components: NightIQA-Real, a real-world dataset of 1,769 high-resolution images that we captured ourselves with modern equipment, encompassing six canonical distortion types and structured multi-dimensional annotations; NightIQA-Bench, a benchmark of 1,078 visually grounded multiple-choice questions tailored to MLLM-based nighttime IQA, organized around a four-level evaluation hierarchy spanning Perception, Technical Assessment, Localization, and Reasoning; and NightIQA-Syn, an inherently scalable, scene-aware synthesis pipeline that jointly models global-level and instance-level degradations, with an initial release of 80k high-fidelity images alongside the full generation code. Fine-tuned on NightIQA with Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) and Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), Qwen3-VL-8B outperforms open-source IQA methods and achieves higher overall accuracy than leading closed-source models, highlighting the value of domain-specific data and structured supervision.

papers.title: NightIQA: A Comprehensive Dataset and Benchmark for MLLM-Based Nighttime Image Quality Assessment

papers.abstract: Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) often process hundreds or thousands of visual tokens, resulting in substantial computational and memory overhead during inference. Existing training-free pruning methods typically estimate token importance using language-model attention, visual attention, or feature similarity. However, these methods treat visual tokens with uniform criteria and overlook that tokens may serve different roles during visual encoding. In this work, we investigate the evolution of visual token roles in LVLMs and observe that tokens progressively transition from local detail carriers to globally referenced representatives as encoding proceeds. Based on this observation, we propose BtsPruner, a training-free role-aware visual token pruning framework that preserves complementary token roles under a fixed budget. Specifically, BtsPruner first identifies the token-role transition point based on the evolution of attention concentration. It then discovers globally referenced representatives from later encoding stages and recursively retrieves local detail tokens from earlier stages to recover complementary fine-grained evidence. Extensive experiments across LLaVA-1.5, LLaVA-NeXT, Qwen-VL, InternVL, and CogVLM demonstrate that BtsPruner achieves superior performance retention under aggressive token reduction. On LLaVA-1.5-7B, BtsPruner preserves 91.6% of the dense model's performance using only 32 of 576 visual tokens (5.6%). In the high-resolution LLaVA-NeXT-7B setting, it achieves up to a 5.95x CUDA-latency speedup.
authors: Zihao Qi, Zhibo Zhang, Miaoxin Zhang, Jincheng Cai, Zengqiang Yan
bullets: LVLM inference is costly because it processes hundreds or thousands of visual tokens.
The method observes that tokens evolve from local detail carriers to globally referenced representatives during encoding.
It identifies this role-transition point, selects global representatives from later stages, and recursively retrieves complementary local tokens from earlier stages.
Across multiple LVLMs, it retains strong performance under substantial token reduction.
On LLaVA-1.5-7B, it retains 91.6% of dense-model performance with 32/576 tokens; on LLaVA-NeXT-7B, it provides up to 5.95× CUDA-latency speedup.

papers.title: BtsPruner: Role-Aware Visual Token Pruning for Large Vision-Language Models

papers.abstract: Time-series interpretation often requires both numerical observations and textual context. Integrating these inputs into a pretrained language model raises a representation question: how should a signal enter the model's token sequence? We present TEMPO, which extends an LLM's vocabulary with discrete codes from a context-aware Transformer tokenizer using finite scalar quantization. A frozen tokenizer maps four-step patches to a 625-code vocabulary; signal tokens, scale statistics, and text are then processed by the LLM's existing self-attention layers. Adaptation updates the new token embeddings and DoRA adapters. With a Qwen3-4B backbone and task-specific fine-tuning, TEMPO achieves macro-F1 scores of 89.0% on activity recognition, 85.0% on sleep staging, and 86.0% on bearing-fault diagnosis. Time-series question answering and qualitative bearing-diagnosis examples further illustrate how this interface combines signal representations with textual context. Together, these results demonstrate the utility of discrete vocabulary extension for time-series understanding.
bullets: Addresses how numerical signals can be integrated into pretrained language-model token sequences.
Uses a context-aware Transformer tokenizer with finite scalar quantization to encode four-step patches into 625 discrete codes.
Combines signal tokens, scale statistics, and text through the LLM’s existing self-attention layers.
Adapts the model by training new token embeddings and DoRA adapters while keeping the tokenizer frozen.
Reports macro-F1 scores of 89.0% for activity recognition, 85.0% for sleep staging, and 86.0% for bearing-fault diagnosis; also demonstrates time-series question answering.

papers.abstract: Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) routinely name objects that are absent from the image. Latent steering can reduce this failure in one model forward pass, but a fixed gate treats early and late decoding steps by the same criterion. We observe that predictive entropy varies sharply within free-running generation, while states that commit to short answers occupy a narrow, confident band. We exploit this temporal mismatch by using uncertainty as a causally available, token-local control signal for an existing steering gate. We propose Entropy-Gated Dynamic Rectification (EGDR), which lowers the intervention threshold when entropy derived from the preceding step's already available logits is high and retains the calibrated operating point when it is low. On LLaVA-1.5-7B, the underlying static gate lowers CHAIR CS/CI from 53.00/15.30 to 32.00/14.30; replacing only its constant threshold with EGDR further lowers them to 29.00/13.60. At a matched 58% intervention rate, the corresponding static control obtains 30.50/14.00. The gain over the static gate holds on LLaVA-NeXT-7B and grows with the generation budget, while POPE scores and general multimodal capability remain effectively unchanged. EGDR requires no additional model forward pass and adds roughly 2% measured latency. Our code is available at https://github.com/alvi-uiu/EGDR.
authors: Riasad Alvi, Md. Asaduzzaman Shuvo, Md. Ahashan Habib, Md. Faiyaz Abdullah Sayeedi
bullets: Targets object hallucination caused by LVLMs naming objects absent from images.
Adjusts an existing steering gate using entropy from the preceding step’s available logits: higher uncertainty triggers stronger intervention.
On LLaVA-1.5-7B, reduces CHAIR CS/CI from 32.00/14.30 with a static gate to 29.00/13.60 with EGDR.
The improvement also holds on LLaVA-NeXT-7B and increases with the generation budget.
Maintains POPE and general multimodal performance, adding roughly 2% measured latency.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Pipeline of EGDR. (a) Held-out calibration selects the steering depth ℓ∗, estimates the prior-removed direction v(ℓ∗), threshold τ , and entropy band [Hlo, Hhi], and tunes α and wτ . (b) At each decoding step, the current hidden state yields risk Rt, while preceding-step entropy lowers τ to τeff. If Rt > τeff, EGDR injects αv(ℓ∗). This requires no additional forward pass or trained parameter. (c) The adaptive threshold admits states missed by the static gate; at the first token, ê = 0 and τeff = τ .

Figure 1. Overview of EGDR. Both gates share v, ℓ∗ and α; only the threshold differs. (a) A static gate applies one threshold τ at every step. (b) EGDR lowers it to τeff(t) using the entropy of the preceding step’s logits, rescaled to the calibrated band, and so corrects states the static gate misses; at t=1, ê=0 and τeff=τ . papers.selection_reason: Reduces object hallucination in large vision-language models via entropy-gated steering; directly relevant to multimodal LLMs.
papers.title: Entropy-Gated Dynamic Rectification for Object Hallucination in Large Vision-Language Models
papers.tldr: EGDR uses token-level predictive entropy to dynamically control latent steering, reducing object hallucinations in LVLMs without extra forward passes or meaningful capability loss.

papers.abstract: Language models are accurate on most long-arithmetic problems, but their accuracy is estimated on samples and carries no guarantee for an unseen input; tool use is exact but moves the computation outside the network. We show that exactness at all input lengths becomes a finite, checkable property of a network when each of its steps reads only a bounded view of an external working memory. In Sketchpad, Qwen3.5-0.8B with a low-rank adapter executes arithmetic procedures on a rendered sheet. Each forward pass reads a three-cell view and emits one step: a digit, a carry or borrow, and the next operation. A fixed runtime moves the view and writes no digit of a result. We prove in Lean that the model is then exact on all inputs of any length if and only if it is exact on the finite set of views the runtime presents, that no finite test suffices when steps also read earlier steps, and that the guarantee tolerates bounded numerical perturbation and extends to compositions of procedures. All 2,446 views pass on the deployment device, a laptop GPU running the model in a web browser. The certified model performs signed addition and subtraction, long multiplication and division, square roots and greatest common divisors at arbitrary length. It solved 200 of 200 pre-registered problems in the browser, and 220 of 220 sums of up to 1,000 digits and products of up to 20 digits, of which GPT-6.1 Sol, the strongest of ten other models, solved 217. A symbolic runtime built on these procedures solves, expands and factors polynomials with every number computed by the model, and a multiplicative gate on the adapter recovers the base model exactly when the sheet is not in use.
bullets: Addresses the lack of guarantees for language-model arithmetic and the externalization of tool-based computation.
Uses Qwen3.5-0.8B with a low-rank adapter; each pass reads three cells and emits a digit, carry/borrow, and next operation, while fixed runtime controls the sheet.
A Lean proof reduces correctness for all input lengths to checking the finite set of views presented by the runtime; this does not hold when steps access earlier outputs.
All 2,446 deployment views passed, and the model handled signed arithmetic, multiplication, division, square roots, and greatest common divisors at arbitrary length.
The system solved all reported browser test problems and supports symbolic polynomial operations, while a multiplicative adapter gate preserves the base model when arithmetic is unused.

The view (three cells, 32 × 96 pixels) enters Qwen3.5-0.8B as three image tokens after the operation token MUL; the outputs, read at = and two placeholder positions, are the digit, the carry and the next operation. The smallest margin, 3.02 logits, belongs to the addition view 5 + 6 with no incoming carry. c, Exact answers on the pre-registered comparison of 220 problems (sums of 10–1,000 digits and products of 2–20-digit numbers, 20 per length; Methods), overall and on the longest sums and products. Fig. 6 | Mechanism. Arithmetic adapter. a, Logit lens: fraction of views whose top token at each depth equals the final output, by operation; ticks mark the median decision depth, triangles the ends of full-attention layers. b, Final-layer states projected onto three discriminant directions, coloured by output, for addition (0–19) and multiplication digits; nearest-centre shares are measured in this projection (Methods). c, Fraction of 80 steps whose output a class-mean intervention changes to its target, against the depth at which it is applied, for addition and multiplication; the shaded band is the fifth full-attention layer.

Fig. 3 | Certification. a, Sums of increasing length read only views from the 242-view addition table; nine sums of 4 to 1,024 digits reach 202 of them. b, The counterexample of Theorem 2: with state in the context, a decoder passes all tests up to N steps and fails at step N + 1 (N = 4, 8, 16; the sink score satisfies ec = 2N + 3, Appendix A); under the pinned-sheet policy the margin is constant. c, Margins of all 2,446 views on the M4, by operation; dark points mark the lowest tenth, which is rechecked on each new device. d, Smallest margin per operation on the server (PyTorch, 32-bit) against the browser (WebGPU): 16-bit decoders lie on the identity line; 4-bit decoders of preliminary adapters deviate by up to 3 logits.

papers.selection_reason: Small vision-language model with certified exact arithmetic on rendered working memory; fits multimodal LLM/VLM research.
papers.title: Sketchpad: certified exact arithmetic with a small vision-language model
papers.tldr: Sketchpad certifies arbitrary-length exact arithmetic by having a small vision-language model process a bounded local view of a rendered working sheet at each step.

papers.abstract: Promptable perception, from GroundingDINO to Rex-Omni, puts one model behind one prompt interface and returns coordinates for any localisation task. Every model in that line was built for photographs; none has been given a sketch. We present Sketch-Omni, to our knowledge the first perception MLLM built to work on sketches and from them. On a sketch, the sketch is the image, and text prompts detect, point, resolve object and spatial referring expressions, and ground affordances in it. From a sketch, the sketch is the prompt, and a drawing of one object localises that object in a photograph, even among several of the same category, a query that neither a category name nor a photo exemplar can pose. Two obstacles stand in the way. A photo-trained model's attention is tuned to colour and texture, which a sketch does not have, and no dataset pairs a drawing with the one instance it depicts among others of its kind. We build the training data instead of collecting it. An edge detector turns every labelled photograph into a sketch-like drawing that keeps the photograph's labels, and two constructions produce sketch-to-photo instance pairs from existing data. On top of this, photo-guided relation alignment passes each photograph and its edge sketch through the same model and trains the sketch pass to reproduce how the photograph pass relates phrases to patches and patches to each other. Not one training label is drawn by hand. Sketch-Omni reaches 91.4 F1 on sketch-prompted localisation against 81.8 for the strongest general-purpose MLLM, with a lead that doubles when the photograph holds several instances of the queried category, and it is best in 39 of 40 evaluation cells across six tasks. Code, model, and a hand-annotated benchmark of 2754 sketch-to-photo links will be released.
authors: Dongyu Wang, Dar-Yen Chen, Zhiming Hong, Arkaprabha Basu, Yi-Zhe Song
bullets: Addresses the lack of sketch-capable perception models and the difficulty of identifying one instance among multiple same-category objects.
Builds training data automatically by converting labelled photos into edge sketches and constructing sketch-to-photo instance pairs from existing datasets.
Uses photo-guided relation alignment to transfer phrase–patch and patch–patch relationships from photographs to sketches.
Achieves 91.4 F1 on sketch-prompted localisation versus 81.8 for the strongest general-purpose MLLM, with larger gains in multi-instance scenes.
Performs best in 39 of 40 evaluation cells across six tasks; a hand-annotated benchmark of 2,754 sketch-to-photo links is planned for release.

papers.title: Sketch-Omni: Instance-Level Sketch-Based Visual Prompting for Perception MLLMs
papers.tldr: Sketch-Omni enables perception MLLMs to understand sketches as images and use object sketches as instance-specific prompts for localising matching objects in photographs.

papers.abstract: Cross-Domain Few-Shot Segmentation (CD-FSS) aims to segment objects from unseen domains using only a few annotated references. Recent Segment Anything Model (SAM)-based methods have advanced CD-FSS, yet their reference-target visual matching is highly sensitive to target appearance variations. SAM3 introduces text-conditioned segmentation, enabling natural-language descriptions to guide segmentation across target images, but directly using the category name as the condition still yields unstable performance under severe domain shifts. We propose Reference Inversion for SAM3 (RI-SAM3) that leverages SAM3's large-scale vision-language pre-training to learn suitable textual tokens for each target category. RI-SAM3 comprises three core designs: (i) Bi-level Reference Inversion that learns complementary tokens before and after the frozen text encoder: the former remain anchored in SAM3's text space while the latter represent the category more flexibly; (ii) Layer-adaptive Textual Conditioning combines these tokens differently as object queries evolve across decoder layers; and (iii) Presence-aware Confidence Supervision that jointly supervises query confidence and target presence for reliable predictions. With SAM3 frozen, RI-SAM3 optimizes around 12K parameters only per category and it efficiently segments each target in a single forward pass with reusable textual conditioning without per-sample reference-target visual matching. Extensive experiments over multiple widely adopted benchmarks show that RI-SAM3 achieves superior performance consistently in CD-FSS tasks, together with strong robustness, efficiency, and generalization.
authors: Jiahao Nie, Yun Xing, Wenbin An, Qixin Zhang, Yap-Peng Tan, Alex C. Kot, Shijian Lu
bullets: Addresses unstable SAM-based segmentation under severe domain shifts and target appearance variation.
Learns complementary category tokens before and after SAM3’s frozen text encoder through bi-level reference inversion.
Uses layer-adaptive textual conditioning and presence-aware confidence supervision for more reliable predictions.
Optimizes only about 12K parameters per category and segments targets in one forward pass without per-sample visual matching.
Experiments across multiple benchmarks report consistently superior performance, robustness, efficiency, and generalization.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of our proposed RI-SAM3 framework. Bi-level Reference Inversion (BRI) learns reference word tokens z∗w and reference concept tokens z∗c from annotated references, collectively termed inverted reference tokens. Layer-adaptive Textual Conditioning (LTC) combines them with layer-specific fusion coefficients α∗ to produce the bi-level reference tokens T ∗ c for conditioning frozen SAM3. Presence-aware Confidence Supervision (PCS) jointly supervises query-level classification and global presence scores. Once learned, T ∗ c is reused for target segmentation without references or visual matching.

Figure 1: Motivation for Reference Inversion for SAM3 (RI-SAM3). Left: Using the same reference image, GF-SAM (Zhang et al. 2024a) exhibits substantial IoU variations across different target images, while manually specified text prompts produce low and unstable results under severe domain shifts. Our proposed RI-SAM3 instead inverts annotated references into a reusable textual condition for inference targets. Right: RI-SAM3 achieves higher mIoU (↑) and a lower standard deviation of per-image IoU (↓) than GF-SAM and the category-name prompt baseline, demonstrating improved accuracy and stability.

papers.title: From Visual Matching to Textual Conditioning: Cross-Domain Few-Shot Segmentation via Reference Inversion
papers.tldr: RI-SAM3 improves cross-domain few-shot segmentation by learning category-specific textual tokens instead of relying on fragile visual reference-target matching.

papers.abstract: Large foundation models often answer even when the available visual or textual evidence is insufficient to support a reliable conclusion. This failure to abstain makes them hard to trust in high-stakes or information-seeking settings, where a confident but unsupported answer can be worse than no answer at all. It also raises a natural question: can the internal mechanisms behind this behaviour be identified and controlled at inference time? We present Dr. No, a feature-steering approach that mines sparse autoencoder (SAE) features associated with abstention and commitment, then modulates a small set of them during the prefill pass, without retraining the base model. Dr. No is evaluated on LLaVA-1.6 Mistral 7B across multimodal abstention benchmarks, including UNK-VQA and MM-UPD, and additionally benchmarked on language reasoning tasks using Qwen3.5-2B on AbstentionBench subsets. Against multiple uncertainty-based abstention baselines, feature steering achieves a more favourable balance between correct answering and appropriate abstention than post-hoc rejection methods. The gains are strongest on UNK-VQA and on MM-UPD cases involving image--question or question--answer incompatibility, and transfer most clearly to mathematical reasoning subsets of AbstentionBench. However, performance is more limited on absent-answer detection and retrieval-heavy multi-hop QA, such as MuSiQue. These results suggest that sparse internal features provide lightweight control handles for shaping uncertainty-aware behaviour in foundation models, while also showing that abstention control is source-dependent rather than governed by a single universal signal.

papers.abstract: Multimodal language models continue to improve on broad music understanding benchmarks, but which musical features can they perceive and reason about? We investigate this question by introducing PianoBench, a benchmark that tasks language models with reasoning about musical performances across congruent acoustic and symbolic input representations. PianoBench is derived from our new multimodal, training-scale dataset comprising more than 20,000 hours of interleaved transcripts of music and spoken musical commentary from instructional piano videos. Open-weight audio-language models achieve at most 52.8% accuracy on PianoBench, and at best only modestly outperform their accuracy on a no-audio control. In contrast, frontier models using chain of thought achieve up to 93.2% accuracy when provided transcripts of music as text, exposing a gap between perceiving musical features from audio and reasoning about musical events when they are given explicitly. We then test whether mid-training on interleaved musical instruction can improve question answering without chain of thought, raising Qwen 3.5 9B Base's zero-shot accuracy on PianoBench with music transcripts from 42.8% to 56.0% after instruction tuning. These experiments suggest that instructional videos may represent an overlooked source of multimodal supervision for music. Available: https://gclef-cmu.org/pianobench.
authors: Louis Bradshaw, Irmak Bukey, Daniel Chenyu Lin, John Thickstun, Chris Donahue

papers.abstract: Injecting non-text modalities into frozen language models often introduces early optimization instability, making it difficult to separate architectural gains from transient training dynamics. We introduce Inductively Gated Cross-Attention (IGCA), a zero-initialized cross-attention bridge that preserves pretrained model behavior at initialization while enabling gradual multimodal conditioning. Integrated across six decoder layers of frozen Falcon-40B, open_llama_30b, and Bloom-7b1 backbones (with 40,404,961,288 trainable adapter parameters used during training), IGCA acts as an exact algebraic no-op at initialization with a maximum output discrepancy of 0.00e+00. Over 59,500 training steps on Falcon-40B, the training loss decreases from 3.9403 to 0.0007 (with final ten step losses of [0.0001, 0.0003, 0.0005, 0.0002, 0.0005, 0.0011, 0.0005, 0.0006, 0.0005, 0.0007]). On held-out evaluation, the best gate-on checkpoint achieves a loss of 2.2201 compared to 4.3469 for the gate-off baseline -- a 48.9% reduction (2.1268 nats) -- while average held-out loss improves from 4.3423 to 2.2498 (1.9075 nats) with a mean gate magnitude of $\vert{}\tanh(\alpha)\vert{} = 0.0713$.
bullets: Addresses early optimization instability when adding non-text modalities to frozen language models.
Uses zero-initialized, learnable gated cross-attention inserted across six decoder layers.
At initialization, the bridge preserves pretrained behavior exactly, with reported output discrepancy of 0.00e+00.
On Falcon-40B held-out evaluation, gate-on performance improves loss from 4.3469 to 2.2201 versus the gate-off baseline.
The approach is evaluated with frozen Falcon-40B, open_llama_30b, and Bloom-7b backbones; results reported primarily for Falcon-40B.

papers.abstract: Omni-modal large language models (LLMs) have achieved remarkable progress in audio and video understanding. However, existing models struggle with long-form, multi-speaker videos, especially in understanding the entire video and recognizing who says what and when. To characterize the capability limit of current omni LLMs and guide future model development, we introduce Omnilingual-MsASR, a multilingual, multimodal benchmark for long-form Multi-speaker Automatic Speech Recognition (MsASR) covering six languages, recordings up to 30 minutes, and scenarios with up to 20 speakers. Omnilingual-MsASR provides parallel audio and video inputs to evaluate models' cross-modal consistency and their ability to exploit complementary cues across modalities. Extensive evaluations of leading omni-modal LLMs reveal substantial performance bottlenecks, while their tcpWERs frequently exceed 100%. These findings highlight fine-grained temporal localization, speaker disambiguation, and cross-modal synergy as key challenges for future omni-modal foundation models. Our work is available at https://github.com/QwenLM/Omnilingua-Bench/tree/main/Omnilingua-MSpeaker.
bullets: Covers six languages, recordings up to 30 minutes, and scenarios with up to 20 speakers.
Provides parallel audio and video inputs to assess cross-modal consistency and complementary information use.
Evaluations of leading omni-modal LLMs show substantial performance bottlenecks, with tcpWER frequently exceeding 100%.

papers.abstract: Multi-step visual retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) answers complex questions by repeatedly retrieving visual evidence, updating an intermediate state, and deciding whether to continue searching or answer. Yet retrieving relevant evidence does not ensure its effective use throughout the reasoning trajectory. As multi-step reasoning progresses, redundant sources occupy context capacity needed for missing evidence, observations tied to resolved requirements or unproductive searches linger in context, and visual sources are revisited with insufficient detail for fine-grained reading. We term this loss of usable evidence over a reasoning trajectory trajectory-level evidence utilization degradation. To address it, we propose Trajectory-Aware Evidence Coordination (TAEC), a training-free framework that coordinates evidence use around unresolved answer requirements. TAEC tracks these requirements in a shared trajectory state to guide which evidence enters the context, how accumulated memory is retained, and at what level of detail visual evidence is examined. Under a unified evaluation protocol on ViDoSeek, SlideVQA, and MMLongBench-Doc, TAEC achieves the best overall performance against leading training-free visual RAG baselines, with the highest average accuracy across multiple proprietary vision-language models. These results demonstrate that aligning evidence with evolving reasoning needs improves evidence use throughout multi-step visual RAG.
bullets: Addresses trajectory-level evidence utilization degradation, where redundant, outdated, or insufficiently detailed evidence hinders ongoing reasoning.
Uses a shared trajectory state to track unresolved answer requirements.
Guides context inclusion, memory retention, and the visual-detail level used for evidence examination.
A training-free framework evaluated on ViDoSeek, SlideVQA, and MMLongBench-Doc.
Reports the best overall performance among leading training-free visual RAG baselines across multiple proprietary vision-language models.

papers.abstract: Unified Multimodal Models (UMMs) achieve remarkable success on diverse multimodal understanding and generation tasks, yet they still struggle to effectively leverage language-based chain-of-thought reasoning for image generation. As a result, existing reasoning-augmented UMMs often fail to inherit the test-time scaling and fine-grained controllability observed in large language models. We attribute this failure to a fundamental modality mismatch: reasoning is performed in a discrete token space, whereas image generation operates in a continuous space. To bridge this gap, we introduce a Latent Reasoning framework in Continuous space (LARC), which alleviates the token-level bottleneck by reasoning over continuous hidden states. Specifically, the training framework consists of two stages: (i) curriculum supervised fine-tuning (SFT), and (ii) information-gain reinforcement learning (RL). First, the curriculum SFT stage gradually converts token-level reasoning into latent reasoning. Subsequently, the information-gain RL stage self-evolves latent reasoning without ground truth supervision. Experiments across diverse text-to-image generation benchmarks show that LARC consistently improves generation quality, prompt following, and compositional fidelity. Notably, LARC achieves state-of-the-art performance on GenEval with a 7%p gain over BAGEL and demonstrates clear test-time scaling behavior, outperforming token-based generation under both parallel and sequential test-time scaling strategies.
authors: Byungwoo Jeon, Yoonwoo Jeong, Hyunseok Lee, Minsu Cho, Jinwoo Shin
bullets: Addresses the mismatch between discrete language reasoning and continuous image generation.
Uses curriculum supervised fine-tuning to transition from token-level to latent reasoning.
Applies information-gain reinforcement learning to develop latent reasoning without ground-truth supervision.
Improves generation quality, prompt following, and compositional fidelity across text-to-image benchmarks.
Achieves a 7-percentage-point GenEval gain over BAGEL and outperforms token-based reasoning under parallel and sequential test-time scaling.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of LARC. Our framework, LARC, consists of two stages. (1) Stage 1 adapts supervised fine-tuning (SFT) while gradually introducing latent thought on continuous space where the last hidden state of UMM becomes the next input embedding of the model. papers.abstract: A panoramic video captures all directions around the camera, but relevant evidence can appear in different directions and at different times. Understanding it requires models to connect observations across the viewing sphere and time. We introduce PanoVideoBench, the first manually annotated benchmark for comprehensive panoramic video understanding. Its 1,000 questions span five categories and 15 question types, with diagnostic annotations for target search and panoramic capabilities. Evaluation of 11 proprietary, open-source, and panoramic-specialized models identifies cross-view tracking and sphere-time evidence integration as their weakest capabilities. To strengthen these capabilities, we construct PanoVideoCoT, the first reasoning dataset grounded in real panoramic video, through sphere-time-grounded synthesis that converts verified panoramic observations and successful agentic explorations into 13,465 QA-CoT pairs. Starting from a general video MLLM, PanoVideoReasoner learns from this corpus through Panoramic CoT SFT and Evidence-Privileged On-Policy Self-Distillation, a panoramic instantiation of Vision-OPD's OPSD in which the teacher uses verified perspective views to guide student-generated trajectories. It reaches 55.7% on PanoVideoBench, improving the backbone by 12.5 points and the previous SOTA by 2.6. The gains concentrate on the same spatial, cross-view, and temporal capabilities exposed by the benchmark, showing that grounded sphere-time supervision can equip a general video MLLM with panoramic reasoning.
authors: Lidong Lu, Lidong Zou, Xinyi Mao, Jiaxin Lv, Zhenquan Li, Liangrui Dong, Tong Lu, Guo Chen

Trains PanoVideoReasoner using Panoramic CoT SFT and evidence-privileged on-policy self-distillation.
Achieves 55.7% on PanoVideoBench, improving its backbone by 12.5 points and prior state of the art by 2.6 points.

papers.abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have achieved impressive performance across a wide range of reasoning tasks, yet it remains unclear whether their internal representations and decision criteria align with the latent structure of human cognition. In this work, we propose a novel framework to align MLLMs with the multidimensional mental representations underlying human similarity judgements. We build on a previously established behavior-derived semantic embedding space, in which objects are represented along 66 interpretable dimensions derived from 4.70 million human Odd-One-Out (O1O) judgements. For each triplet, we infer the most salient decision dimension and convert it into a dimension-grounded linguistic rationale. This enables MLLMs to learn both the final choice and a justification consistent with the inferred behavioral criterion. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach improves model consistency with human similarity judgements while retaining competitive performance on standard multimodal benchmarks. Furthermore, using searchlight Representational Similarity Analysis (RSA) on an independent fMRI Natural Scenes Dataset (NSD), we observe increased representational alignment between model and human. Ultimately, our findings point to a data-driven route for incorporating human cognitive structure into MLLMs alignment. The code is available \href{https://github.com/ening-open/cogalign}{here}.
authors: Ning E, Changde Du, Yizhuo Lu, Huiguang He

Improves consistency with human similarity judgments while retaining competitive multimodal benchmark performance.

figures.caption: Figure 4: Cortical projection of representational alignment improvements across subjects. The heatmaps visualize the voxel-wise difference in ∆̃RSA(c) scores between the aligned and baseline Qwen3-VL-4B-Instruct model. Darker colors indicate better representational alignment between models and human brain. Consistent positive shifts are observed, demonstrating that our alignment framework robustly shifts the MLLMs internal representational geometry to be more human-like.

Figure 1: Overview of triplet-level semantic dimension attribution. (a) Human similarity judgements are collected via crowdsourcing. Then learning a representational embedding space via SPoSE yields the multidimensional mental representations of natural objects. (b) For one triplet, we compute the original softmax probability based on the entire representational embedding for all pairs. We then iteratively prune each dimension from the representational embedding space and compute the changes in softmax probabilities relative to those obtained with the full embedding as the relevance score for that dimension. By sorting these relevance scores in descending order, we establish a hierarchical ranking of dimensional importance. The top-1 dimension yielding the maximum probability change is regarded as the most salient semantic dimension driving the human decision-making.

Figure 3: (a) Overview of hybrid dataset. The total dataset includes three subsets: Single-image (126K samples), Multi-image (102K samples), and Cognitive-Alignment (80K samples). (b) Examples. The examples include Spot the Difference, Image Edit Instruction, Visual Storytelling, LLaVAR, COCO Caption, and Odd-One-Out tasks.

Figure 2: Pipeline for dimension-grounded reasoning enhancement. This pipeline illustrates the process of reasoning enhancement via LLM. For one triplet with their textual descriptions and the most salient semantic dimension d∗ driving human decision-making, we integrate them into the structured prompt Prompt(T , cap(T ), d∗). LLM is then utilized exclusively to enhance reasoning. By injecting the dimension d∗, we guide the LLM to perform targeted reasoning enhancement. This effectively converts discrete cognitive criteria for decision-making into explicit CoT rationale r(d∗).

Figure 5: Stability of alignment shifts across different extraction depths. The cortical projections display the alignment improvements ∆̃RSA(c) of subject 1 computed using features from the last layer, the second-to-last layer, and the concatenation of the last four layers. Darker regions reflect better alignment improvement. The spatial distribution of these positive shifts remains consistent regardless of the extraction depth, confirming that the achieved representational alignment with human cognition is robust and not a selective layer choice.

papers.abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) are increasingly capable of understanding images and performing complex visual reasoning, suggesting the possibility of using them to automate biological image analysis. This need is becoming increasingly urgent as advances in technology continue to generate ever larger and more diverse microscopy datasets, already exceeding the scale at which manual visual analysis is feasible. With the final aim to use MLLMs for visual comparison of complex phenotypes, we investigate a very simple baseline: comparison of the size of body parts in synthetic images of ants. We find that state-of-the-art open-weight MLLMs fail for some body parts, but not for others, even though the comparison itself is visually trivial for all of them. We evaluate different in-context learning strategies and analyze performance on the related object recognition task. Our results suggest a recognition-driven grounding failure: structures that the models cannot recognize are instead associated with a recognizable semantic concept, impairing the grounding and comparison of both. Further analysis of the vision encoder is consistent with the hypothesis that fine-grained visual structure may be less well preserved without semantic support. Together, our results reveal a surprising limitation of current MLLMs: semantic recognition can gate simple visual comparisons that do not intrinsically require semantic understanding. Our code and data are available at https://github.com/kreshuklab/Open-Weight-MLLMs-Cannot-Compare-What-They-Cannot-Name

papers.abstract: A central challenge in multimodal in-context learning (MICL) arises from tasks that are ill-defined without context and require uncovering the underlying rules from demonstrations. Existing methods predominantly treat MICL as direct input-output mapping, overlooking the importance of explicitly inducing and reasoning over such rules, limiting both performance and interpretability. We propose ERIM, Explicit Rule-Induction for Multimodal In-Context Learning, a unified framework that enhances MICL by explicitly inducing the latent rules governing demonstration samples. Leveraging the reasoning ability of multi-modal large language model (MLLM), ERIM constructs rule-centric MICL datasets, introduces explicit supervision for rule induction, and fine-tunes MLLM to perform explicit rule-induction via a two-stage training strategy that combines mixed cold-start supervised fine-tuning with reinforcement learning. Extensive experiments show consistent performance improvements across diverse MICL settings and demonstrate that correctly inducing underlying rules directly leads to stronger and more stable performance.
authors: Yuquan Li, Xinyang Jiang, Yuhao Xue, Cairong Zhao
bullets: Addresses ill-defined MICL tasks whose solutions depend on uncovering rules from examples.
Uses multimodal large language models to construct rule-centric data and provide explicit rule-induction supervision.
Trains models in two stages with mixed cold-start supervised fine-tuning followed by reinforcement learning.
Experiments across diverse MICL settings show consistent gains and more stable performance.
The approach focuses on settings where latent rules can be inferred from demonstrations.

papers.abstract: Bridging independent vision-language models (VLMs) and small language models (SLMs) in a modular multi-agent system typically forces them to exchange information as discrete text, which creates a lossy bottleneck for spatial and fine-grained details. This constraint is especially acute for SLMs, whose limited capacity makes them more reliant on the quality of the input signal. Recent latent-communication methods exchange states between language models. How a VLM can pass visual information to a separately pretrained text-only SLM though remains unexplored. We propose \textbf{Latent-Lens}, a lightweight codec that bridges the representation gap between a frozen VLM and a frozen SLM directly in latent space, enabling them to communicate purely through hidden states. The codec consists of a domain encoder that projects hidden states from the VLM into the SLM's embedding space, and an attention decoder formalised as a LoRA that teaches the SLM to attend to these visual prefixes, while training only ${\sim}1.6$M parameters (0.2\% of the combined model size). On visual question answering (CLEVR, GQA), Latent-Lens achieves $81.0\pm7.9$\% and $65.4\pm5.4$\%, compared with $58.3\pm5.7$\% and $61.8\pm1.0$\% for text communication with the same LoRA budget (+30.2--69.8pp relative to frozen text communication), while on image captioning (Flickr8k) it improves over the same baseline by +16.5 (+18.8 frozen). We also evaluate Latent-Lens with TinyLlama-1.1B and InternVL2-1B, which use different architectures, vocabularies, and hidden dimensions.

bullets: Addresses the loss of spatial and fine-grained visual information caused by text-only communication between modular VLMs and SLMs.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) has recently been extended to vision-language models (VLMs), yet its effectiveness remains limited for text-rich reasoning tasks. We highlight a key factor contributing to this limitation: models frequently arrive at correct final answers despite misperceiving visual information during intermediate steps. We define this phenomenon as Correct-but-Visually-Misgrounded Reasoning (CVMR). Because standard RLVR rewards only final-answer correctness, it fails to differentiate between properly grounded and misgrounded reasoning, reinforcing both equally. Through token-level analysis, we reveal that CVMR tokens exhibit distinct attention patterns that differ systematically from well-grounded ones. Based on this observation, we propose GRIT, a training framework that incorporates visual grounding into RLVR to mitigate the impact of CVMR. Furthermore, to address the lack of text-rich reasoning benchmarks that allow for systematic evaluation across text length and reasoning depth, we introduce GRIT-Bench. Experiments demonstrate that GRIT significantly improves both reasoning accuracy and grounding fidelity over existing RLVR methods.
authors: Chanseul Cho, Noori Bae, Dongheon Lee, Youngmin Ro
bullets: Identifies Correct-but-Visually-Misgrounded Reasoning (CVMR), where models answer correctly despite misperceiving visual information during intermediate reasoning.

Introduces GRIT-Bench for evaluating text-rich reasoning across text length and reasoning depth.
Experiments report improved reasoning accuracy and grounding fidelity over existing RLVR methods.

papers.abstract: Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting has become a standard reasoning strategy in Multi-modal Large Language Models (MLLMs), showing strong performance in complex vision-language tasks such as reasoning segmentation. However, our analysis reveals that indiscriminate CoT usage can lead to degraded performance by inducing unnecessary reasoning, a phenomenon we term overthinking. In reasoning segmentation, overthinking often leads to misalignment between the query's intent and visual grounding. To address this, we propose Difficulty-Aware Chain-of-Thought (DA-CoT), a training-free adaptive framework that selectively triggers CoT based on the input's intrinsic difficulty. We find that the entropy of the model's attention maps reliably reflects task difficulty: low entropy indicates confident, localized grounding, while high entropy suggests uncertainty and potential benefit from CoT. DA-CoT uses this entropy signal to determine whether to apply CoT prompting. Additionally, we introduce a Bidirectional Rethinking mechanism that enables the model to automatically flip its reasoning decision when the initial output fails, enhancing robustness by recovering from failures induced by overthinking and underthinking. DA-CoT demonstrates its effectiveness by achieving state-of-the-art performance on the Reasoning Segmentation benchmarks while significantly improving inference efficiency.
authors: Chanseul Cho, Jaesung Jun, Dongheon Lee, Youngmin Ro
bullets: Problem: Always-on CoT can cause overthinking, misaligning visual grounding with the query.
Method: Estimate input difficulty from attention-map entropy; high entropy triggers CoT, while low entropy skips it.
Robustness: Bidirectional Rethinking reverses the initial reasoning choice when the output fails.
Results: Achieves state-of-the-art performance on reasoning segmentation benchmarks and improves inference efficiency.
Scope: Training-free adaptive inference for multimodal reasoning segmentation.

figures.caption: Figure 4. Overview of the proposed DA-CoT framework during inference. The aggregated attention entropy Hagg, computed over the pre-identified layers L, is used to adaptively decide whether to trigger CoT reasoning. If Hagg ≥ τ , the model follows the Difficulty-Aware Prompting Path with CoT for structured reasoning; otherwise, it takes the direct path without CoT for efficient inference. When the initial reasoning path fails to produce a valid output, a discrete flipping signal activates the Bidirectional Rethinking Path, enabling re-evaluation and recovery from overthinking or underthinking. The final bounding boxes or point prompts are then passed to the segmentation head to produce the reasoningaware segmentation result.

papers.abstract: Multimodal indirect prompt injection embeds malicious instructions in external media that also contains information needed for the user's task. Existing defenses can block the attack yet impair the model's use of that information, leaving a gap between attack defense and task preservation. We propose ERASE, an on-policy self-distillation method that constructs its reference by erasing the injected region in place. Modality-appropriate blank content replaces the injection while the surrounding media is preserved. A student reading attacked media learns from a frozen base model reading the erased view through full-distribution token-level feedback on its own rollouts. Across image, audio, and video on two model sizes, ERASE records near-zero observed attack success on the evaluated benchmark while retaining task utility close to the undefended clean-input level. On 3B audio, ERASE reaches 60.1% attacked-input accuracy compared with ARGUS's 33.1%, within 0.5 points of the undefended clean-input level. Experiments show that ERASE reduces injection dependence from 6.26 to 0.0095 on 3B audio while staying close to the base model on the erased input. Out-of-domain accuracy also stays near the base level. Our code will be made publicly available upon acceptance.
authors: Shuo Hong, Jiaxin Ma, Xidi Cai, Qianli Ma
bullets: Addresses the trade-off between blocking malicious instructions and retaining useful information from attacked media.
Uses on-policy self-distillation: a student processes attacked inputs while learning token-level behavior from a frozen base model viewing the erased version.
Evaluated across image, audio, and video with two model sizes, achieving near-zero observed attack success while maintaining near-clean-input task utility.
On 3B audio, ERASE achieves 60.1% attacked-input accuracy versus ARGUS's 33.1%, within 0.5 points of the undefended clean-input level.
Reduces injection dependence from 6.26 to 0.0095 on 3B audio, with out-of-domain accuracy near the base model level.

papers.abstract: While modern Vision-Language Models (VLMs) have been remarkably successful in general scene text recognition, they consistently struggle with the long-tail distribution of text that is degraded by motion blur or low resolution. These limitations are particularly apparent in egocentric applications like smart glasses, where text is often captured in noisy environments. In this paper, we introduce the \textbf{BSTRB} (Blurry Scene Text Recognition Benchmark), a novel benchmark of 8,398 noisy image samples with high-fidelity annotations derived from 1,699 real-world video sequences. To support this, we present \textbf{Hawkeye}, a VLM fine-tuned on BSTRB to read and reason about illegible text by leveraging contextual priors and pixel-level alignment. Our results show that \name matches much larger VLMs on BSTRB overall and exceeds them on text at or below 20 pixels, in a single pass suited to real-time deployment. We characterize the resolution at which current VLMs begin to fail.
bullets: Introduces BSTRB, a benchmark of 8,398 noisy text images from 1,699 real-world video sequences with high-fidelity annotations.
Fine-tunes Hawkeye on BSTRB to read illegible text under motion blur and low resolution.
Hawkeye matches much larger VLMs overall and outperforms them on text at or below 20 pixels.
Characterizes the resolution threshold where current VLMs begin to fail.
Scope: focuses on degraded scene text, especially conditions relevant to smart glasses and other egocentric settings.

papers.abstract: Voice-interactive large language models process both what a speaker says and how they say it, yet the two channels do not always agree. We ask whether that disagreement degrades speech emotion recognition. Mapping text and audio into a shared valence-arousal-dominance space, we convert the distance between them into a continuous, threshold-free incongruence score with a two-component Gaussian mixture, and validate the score against human judgement. We evaluate three audiocapable models on acted, conversational and spontaneous speech (eNTERFACE'05, MELD and CMU-MOSEI). With the model held constant across modalities, incongruence raises the odds of error whenever audio is present, in every corpus, after controlling for the ground-truth emotion and for distance in the feature space. Supervised classifiers trained on the same features behave in the opposite way, which suggests that the difficulty lies in how these models combine raw evidence rather than in the signal itself. Text-only effects are unreliable: swapping only the model that reads the transcript reverses their sign on one corpus. Rebuilding the score without the emotion lexicon reproduces the central result, and among six simpler alternatives it is the only label-free score that predicts error in all three corpora. Code, data tables and prompts are released.
bullets: The study introduces a continuous, threshold-free incongruence score by measuring text–audio distance in valence–arousal–dominance space.
The score is validated against human judgments and tested across acted, conversational, and spontaneous speech using three audio-capable models.
Audio-related incongruence increases prediction errors across all three corpora, even after controlling for ground-truth emotion and feature-space distance.
Supervised classifiers show the opposite pattern, implicating how audio-language models combine evidence rather than the underlying signal.
Text-only effects are inconsistent across models; a lexicon-free version of the score preserves the central finding and outperforms simpler label-free alternatives in consistency.

papers.abstract: A capable voice assistant must do more than recognize words; it must understand requests, reason over context, sustain conversations, and act through tools. We present Apriel Voice 27B Preview, an open speech-language model that unifies these capabilities within a shared reasoning backbone while retaining text and image input modalities. Built on the post-trained Gemma 4 26B-A4B checkpoint, Apriel Voice directly processes speech and generates both responses and tool calls without requiring a separate dialogue model. We introduce a two-stage training procedure to adapt the model to speech. The first stage establishes the speech interface, while the second jointly adapts the projector and backbone through supervised fine-tuning, text replay, and source-dependent cross-entropy and forward Kullback--Leibler divergence supervision. Automatically constructed speech-conditioned dialogues provide conversational training data, while local teacher serving, overlapping teacher and student computation, and fused full-vocabulary losses enable efficient online distillation. In thinking mode, Apriel Voice achieves a score of 98.90 on Big Bench Audio, 81.13 on Speech-BFCL, and a task success rate of 65.51% on $\tau$-Voice, with a mean latency of 1.91 seconds. It also achieves 51.27% English EVA accuracy and 74.13% experience pass@1. Finally, we deploy Apriel Voice 27B Preview on a custom serving platform to support interactive voice interactions.

bullets: Supports speech, text, and image inputs while generating natural-language responses and tool calls.
Uses a two-stage speech adaptation process combining supervised fine-tuning, text replay, and distillation-based losses.
Trains on automatically constructed speech-conditioned dialogues with efficiency optimizations for online teacher–student distillation.
Reports strong performance across Big Bench Audio, Speech-BFCL, τ-Voice, English EVA, and experience pass@1, with 1.91-second mean latency in thinking mode.
Deployed on a custom serving platform for interactive voice conversations.

papers.abstract: Detailed image captioning is usually framed as an amount problem: a model should mention more visual facts while avoiding hallucination. However, autoregressive VLMs generate captions as ordered sequences, and later generations may be produced under weaker or noisier visual grounding. We therefore argue that long-form captioning should be studied not only by what facts are mentioned, but also by where they appear. We introduce a position-aware rubric representation that decomposes dense human references into atomic visual claims, verifies generated captions against those claims, and induces a quartile-wise composition of supported, hallucinated, and generic content. This lens reveals two qualitatively different failures in long captions: models tend to produce unsupported specificity in the middle, while the final portion often escapes into vague, non-evidential language rather than simply accumulating more hallucination. A same-reference human control does not exhibit these patterns; additional human audits examine the visual validity of the induced labels. Motivated by this diagnosis, we propose PAGER (Position-Aware Grounded Evidence Reinforcement), a GRPO training objective with separate signals for supported fine-grained middle evidence, evidence-bearing tail continuation, claim coverage, and content-aware length control. The result is a closed loop: the same ordered claim representation identifies where long captions fail and supplies the position-specific reward needed to repair those failures. Experiments on detailed-caption benchmarks show that PAGER improves position-wise grounding and pairwise caption preference while preserving competitive global caption quality.
bullets: Long captions often become unsupportedly specific in the middle and vague or non-evidential near the end.
A position-aware rubric decomposes references into atomic visual claims and evaluates supported, hallucinated, and generic content by caption quartile.
PAGER applies position-specific GRPO rewards for grounded middle evidence, evidential tail continuation, claim coverage, and content-aware length.
Experiments show improved position-wise grounding and pairwise caption preference while maintaining competitive overall caption quality.

papers.tldr: Long image captions fail in position-specific ways, and PAGER uses ordered claim analysis with position-aware reinforcement learning to improve grounding and preference.

papers.abstract: Recommender systems often suffer from over-concentrated results when optimized for accuracy, limiting recommendation diversity. While diversity has become an important objective, existing methods still face fundamental limitations from both semantic and structural perspectives. On the one hand, multimodal recommender systems provide rich semantic signals, yet are often treated as auxiliary to ID embeddings, leading to ineffective semantic utilization for diversity. On the other hand, the accuracy--diversity trade-off persists during training, where accuracy gains often come at the cost of diversity. We show that this phenomenon is fundamentally governed by both the structural properties of learned representations and the dynamics of optimization. To address these challenges, we propose MOSS, a unified framework for multimodal decoupling through semantic and structural shaping. Specifically, we first introduce an MLLM-based Decoupled Feature Extraction module to disentangle multimodal content into informative representations. To enhance semantic utilization, we design a Category-aware Embedding Selection module that extracts compact, category-aware semantic features. To address structural limitations, we propose two complementary modules: Alternating Dual-Graph Propagation, which alleviates representation collapse by integrating collaborative and multimodal propagation, and Entropy-based Diversity Regularization, which mitigates optimization bias by promoting balanced category exposure. Extensive experiments on real-world datasets demonstrate that MOSS consistently achieves a superior accuracy--diversity trade-off over strong baselines.
bullets: Targets over-concentrated recommendations and the persistent accuracy–diversity trade-off.
Uses MLLM-based decoupled feature extraction and category-aware semantic selection to better exploit multimodal content.
Combines alternating dual-graph propagation with entropy-based regularization to reduce representation collapse and balance category exposure.
Experiments on real-world datasets show a consistently better accuracy–diversity trade-off than strong baselines.

The Category-aware Embedding Selection module selects compact, category-aware features to enhance semantic utilization. The Alternating Dual-Graph Propagation module alleviates dimensional collapse via collaborative and multimodal propagation. The Entropy-based Diversity Regularization module promotes balanced category exposure while preserving accuracy.
